before.q: A firm has $100 of producer surplus and a $70 fixed lease cost. Accounting profit is:
before.feedback: Subtract fixed cost from producer surplus.

after.q: A firm earns $500 in revenue. Its explicit variable costs are $280 and its explicit fixed lease cost is $70. The owner also forgoes $40 of income from another job. What is accounting profit, and why is the forgone income treated that way?
options: $110; accounting profit subtracts explicit costs and the $40 forgone income.
$220; accounting profit excludes both the fixed lease and the $40 forgone income.
$190; accounting profit subtracts the lease but adds the $40 forgone income.
$150; accounting profit subtracts explicit costs, so the $40 forgone income is excluded.
after.feedback: Accounting profit is revenue minus explicit costs: $500−$280−$70=$150. The forgone $40 is an implicit opportunity cost used in economic profit, not an additional explicit cost.

3 trades; marginal buyer value $19, marginal seller cost $16
2 trades; marginal buyer value $24, marginal seller cost $11
3 trades; marginal buyer value $9, marginal seller cost $26

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [28, 34, 40, 46, 52]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [45, 37, 53, 41, 49]. Values and costs are in dollars. What would reallocating that one unit, with no transaction cost, do?
options: Leave total surplus unchanged because output does not change.
Raise total surplus by $18 without changing output.
Lower total surplus by $18 because the original recipient loses the item.
Raise total surplus by $46 because the replaced buyer’s value is irrelevant.
after.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $46−$28=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

after.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $46−$28=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

before.q: Marginal willingness to pay for five successive units is [31, 26, 21, 15, 10]; marginal cost is [4, 12, 18, 22, 29]. How many units maximize total surplus, and what is total surplus at that quantity?
options: 2 units and $41
4 units and $37
3 units and $44
3 units and $78
before.feedback: Produce each unit whose marginal value is at least marginal cost. That yields 3 units and $44 in total gains.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [54, 48, 42, 36, 30]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [14, 18, 22, 26, 30]. Values and costs are in dollars. After ranking values and costs, what is the largest quantity that maximizes total surplus, allowing trades with exactly zero marginal surplus?
options: 4 units; it is the largest maximizer because zero-gain trades are inefficient.
5 units; include the first negative-gain trade.
5 units; total surplus $100.
5 units; total surplus $130.
after.feedback: Marginal gains are [40, 30, 20, 10, 0]. 4 trades add positive surplus and the next adds zero. Both quantities tie, but 5 is the largest maximizing quantity.

before.q: For the schedule with marginal values [31, 26, 21, 15, 10] and marginal costs [4, 12, 18, 22, 29], a planner proposes producing one unit beyond the efficient cutoff. What is the effect of that extra unit?
options: It increases total surplus by $7
It only transfers surplus and leaves total surplus unchanged
It must increase total surplus because output rises
It reduces total surplus by $7
before.feedback: The next unit has value $15 and cost $22, so its contribution is negative $7.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [32, 38, 44, 50, 56]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [39, 31, 47, 35, 43]. Values and costs are in dollars. A new handling requirement uses $8 of real resources for every completed trade, in addition to seller cost. What efficient quantity and total surplus follow?
options: 3 units and $45; handling is only a transfer between participants.
3 units and $37; subtract handling only once for the entire market.
2 units and $45; adjust quantity but leave the surplus sum unchanged.
2 units and $24; include handling in each marginal resource-cost comparison.
after.feedback: Subtract $8 from every marginal gain, yielding [17, 7, -3, -13, -23]. Only 2 remain positive; their sum is $24. Real per-trade resources can change both the cutoff and the welfare total.

before.q: Marginal willingness to pay for five successive units is [34, 28, 23, 17, 11]; marginal cost is [8, 14, 20, 26, 32]. How many units maximize total surplus, and what is total surplus at that quantity?
options: 3 units and $43
2 units and $40
4 units and $34
3 units and $85
before.feedback: Produce each unit whose marginal value is at least marginal cost. That yields 3 units and $43 in total gains.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [50, 44, 38, 32, 26]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [15, 19, 23, 27, 31]. Values and costs are in dollars. The efficient allocation currently includes 4 trades. A new buyer could replace the next excluded buyer, with all other values and costs fixed. What minimum willingness to pay would make an additional unit create nonnegative surplus?
options: $31; compare the new buyer’s value with the next-lowest unused seller cost.
$26; the excluded buyer’s old value is the resource cost of adding a unit.
$27; use the cost of the last unit already supplied.
$80; an extra buyer must exceed all surplus already created.
after.feedback: The first 4 low-cost units are already used. The additional unit requires the next seller, at $31; a new buyer value equal to that cost gives zero incremental surplus, and a higher value gives a positive gain.

before.q: For the schedule with marginal values [34, 28, 23, 17, 11] and marginal costs [8, 14, 20, 26, 32], a planner proposes producing one unit beyond the efficient cutoff. What is the effect of that extra unit?
options: It increases total surplus by $9
It reduces total surplus by $9
It only transfers surplus and leaves total surplus unchanged
It must increase total surplus because output rises
before.feedback: The next unit has value $17 and cost $26, so its contribution is negative $9.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [28, 34, 40, 46, 52]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [55, 47, 63, 51, 59]. Values and costs are in dollars. Allocate goods to the highest values using the lowest costs. Which quantity maximizes total surplus, and what is that surplus?
options: 2 units; total surplus $0.
1 units; total surplus $5.
0 units; total surplus $0.
1 units; total surplus $52.
after.feedback: After ranking buyers and sellers, marginal gains are [5, -5, -15, -25, -35]. Sum the 1 positive gains for $5; another trade would lower total surplus.

before.q: Marginal willingness to pay for five successive units is [27, 23, 19, 13, 7]; marginal cost is [3, 10, 16, 21, 25]. How many units maximize total surplus, and what is total surplus at that quantity?
options: 2 units and $37
4 units and $32
3 units and $40
3 units and $69
before.feedback: Produce each unit whose marginal value is at least marginal cost. That yields 3 units and $40 in total gains.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [54, 48, 42, 36, 30]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [39, 43, 47, 51, 55]. Values and costs are in dollars. Exactly 2 units are produced by the cheapest sellers, but the lowest-valued buyer receives one instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. What would reallocating that one unit, with no transaction cost, do?
options: Leave total surplus unchanged because output does not change.
Lower total surplus by $18 because the original recipient loses the item.
Raise total surplus by $18 without changing output.
Raise total surplus by $48 because the replaced buyer’s value is irrelevant.
after.feedback: The relevant buyer-value difference is $48−$30=$18. Production costs and quantity stay fixed, so that increase in use value is the change in total surplus.

before.q: For the schedule with marginal values [27, 23, 19, 13, 7] and marginal costs [3, 10, 16, 21, 25], a planner proposes producing one unit beyond the efficient cutoff. What is the effect of that extra unit?
options: It increases total surplus by $8
It only transfers surplus and leaves total surplus unchanged
It must increase total surplus because output rises
It reduces total surplus by $8
before.feedback: The next unit has value $13 and cost $21, so its contribution is negative $8.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [32, 38, 44, 50, 56]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [24, 16, 32, 20, 28]. Values and costs are in dollars. After ranking values and costs, what is the largest quantity that maximizes total surplus, allowing trades with exactly zero marginal surplus?
options: 4 units; it is the largest maximizer because zero-gain trades are inefficient.
5 units; include the first negative-gain trade.
5 units; total surplus $132.
5 units; total surplus $100.
after.feedback: Marginal gains are [40, 30, 20, 10, 0]. 4 trades add positive surplus and the next adds zero. Both quantities tie, but 5 is the largest maximizing quantity.

before.q: Marginal willingness to pay for five successive units is [33, 29, 24, 16, 8]; marginal cost is [6, 15, 20, 27, 31]. How many units maximize total surplus, and what is total surplus at that quantity?
options: 3 units and $45
2 units and $41
4 units and $34
3 units and $86
before.feedback: Produce each unit whose marginal value is at least marginal cost. That yields 3 units and $45 in total gains.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [50, 44, 38, 32, 26]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [25, 29, 33, 37, 41]. Values and costs are in dollars. A new handling requirement uses $8 of real resources for every completed trade, in addition to seller cost. What efficient quantity and total surplus follow?
options: 2 units and $24; include handling in each marginal resource-cost comparison.
3 units and $45; handling is only a transfer between participants.
3 units and $37; subtract handling only once for the entire market.
2 units and $45; adjust quantity but leave the surplus sum unchanged.
after.feedback: Subtract $8 from every marginal gain, yielding [17, 7, -3, -13, -23]. Only 2 remain positive; their sum is $24. Real per-trade resources can change both the cutoff and the welfare total.

before.q: For the schedule with marginal values [33, 29, 24, 16, 8] and marginal costs [6, 15, 20, 27, 31], a planner proposes producing one unit beyond the efficient cutoff. What is the effect of that extra unit?
options: It increases total surplus by $11
It reduces total surplus by $11
It only transfers surplus and leaves total surplus unchanged
It must increase total surplus because output rises
before.feedback: The next unit has value $16 and cost $27, so its contribution is negative $11.

after.q: 5 buyers each want one unit with values [28, 34, 40, 46, 52]; 5 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [25, 17, 33, 21, 29]. Values and costs are in dollars. The efficient allocation currently includes 4 trades. A new buyer could replace the next excluded buyer, with all other values and costs fixed. What minimum willingness to pay would make an additional unit create nonnegative surplus?
options: $28; the excluded buyer’s old value is the resource cost of adding a unit.
$33; compare the new buyer’s value with the next-lowest unused seller cost.
$29; use the cost of the last unit already supplied.
$80; an extra buyer must exceed all surplus already created.
after.feedback: The first 4 low-cost units are already used. The additional unit requires the next seller, at $33; a new buyer value equal to that cost gives zero incremental surplus, and a higher value gives a positive gain.

before.q: Refer to the graph. What competitive-equilibrium price is shown?
before.feedback: The dashed horizontal guide through E marks the equilibrium price at $14.

after.q: Use the graph with demand intercept $30 and equilibrium E at Q=8, P=$14. A student labels the $112 revenue rectangle as consumer surplus. Which correction is right?
options: Consumer surplus is the $64 triangle above price and below demand; $112 is expenditure transferred to sellers.
Consumer surplus is $112 because every dollar paid is a buyer gain.
Consumer surplus is $32 because the supply intercept determines the buyer triangle.
Consumer surplus is $176 because add the demand triangle to all payments.
after.feedback: The buyer triangle is 0.5×8×(30−14)=$64. The rectangle 8×14=$112 is payment for the goods, not the buyer’s net gain.

before.q: Refer to the graph. What is the equilibrium quantity at point E?
options: 8 units
6 units
12 units
14 units
before.feedback: The dashed vertical guide through E marks the equilibrium quantity at 8 units.

after.q: Use the graph with supply intercept $6 and E at Q=8, P=$14. A lump-sum rule transfers $20 from buyers to sellers without changing quantity, allocation or resource costs. What is producer surplus after the transfer, and what happens to total surplus?
options: Producer surplus rises from $32 to $52; total surplus is unchanged.
Producer surplus rises from $32 to $52; total surplus rises $20.
Producer surplus falls from $32 to $12; total surplus is unchanged.
Producer surplus starts at $112 and rises to $132; total surplus rises $20.
after.feedback: Initial producer surplus is 0.5×8×(14−6)=$32. The $20 transfer raises sellers’ share to $52 and lowers buyers’ share by the same amount, leaving total surplus unchanged.

before.q: Refer to the graph. What total revenue is exchanged at the asymmetric competitive equilibrium?
before.feedback: Equilibrium price is $14 and quantity is 8, so total expenditure and seller revenue are $112.

after.q: In the graph, demand intercepts price at $30, supply at $6 and E is Q=8, P=$14. A report adds the $112 sales revenue to consumer and producer surplus when measuring gains from exchange. What is the correct total and diagnosis?
options: Total surplus is $96; adding revenue double-counts a payment already separating buyer and seller shares.
Total surplus is $208; revenue is an additional benefit beyond consumer and producer surplus.
Total surplus is $112; payments alone measure the gains from exchange.
Total surplus is $64; producer gains should be excluded because sellers receive payments.
after.feedback: CS=0.5×8×16=$64 and PS=0.5×8×8=$32, totaling $96. Revenue is a transfer from buyers to sellers, not an extra resource benefit.

before.q: Refer to the graph. What efficient quantity is identified by the demand-supply intersection?
options: 5 units
8 units
10 units
14 units
before.feedback: The competitive intersection E occurs at Q = 5, where marginal buyer value equals marginal seller cost.

after.q: In the compact graph, straight demand runs from P=$24 to E at Q=5, P=$14; straight supply runs from P=$4 to E. A quota stops production at Q=4, allocating the units efficiently. How much surplus is forgone on the missing output between 4 and 5?
options: $2: at Q=4 demand is $16 and supply $12, so the missing triangle is 0.5×1×4.
$4: multiply the one-unit base by the full $4 height without halving.
$14: every missing unit loses its market price as surplus.
$10: subtract the equilibrium price from the demand intercept without using quantity.
after.feedback: Demand is 24−2Q and supply 4+2Q. Their gap at Q=4 is 16−12=$4 and reaches zero at Q=5. The forgone triangle is $2.

before.q: A price ceiling transfers $22 to buyers, reduces producer surplus $34, and creates $3 of search costs. Total surplus:
before.feedback: The $22 gain to buyers is more than offset by the $34 producer-surplus loss and $3 of search costs: $22 - $34 - $3 = -$15.

after.q: A price ceiling raises consumer surplus by a net $22 before search costs, reduces producer surplus by $34, and creates $3 of real search costs not included in either surplus figure. What is the change in total surplus?
after.feedback: Add the net consumer-surplus change to the producer-surplus change and subtract the separately stated real search cost: $22−$34−$3=−$15. A transfer component alone would not measure the full consumer-surplus change.

before.q: Which statement best defends competitive efficiency?
options: Everyone receives equal surplus
Price is always fair
All value-above-cost units trade and value-below-cost units do not
No policy can ever help
before.feedback: Competitive efficiency requires every unit with buyer value above seller cost to trade, while units with value below cost should not be produced.

after.q: Three feasible units have buyer values $30, $24, $17 and seller costs $10, $18, $21. A rule requires all three to trade. Which policy change increases total surplus, assuming efficient matching and no other costs?
options: Require a fourth unit without any value/cost evidence because more trades always raise total surplus.
Stop all trade because the third unit’s loss proves the first two also lose surplus.
Allow only the first two units: it removes a third-unit loss of $4 while retaining positive gains of $20 and $6.
Keep all three because payments from buyers necessarily cover social opportunity costs.
after.feedback: The three marginal gains are $20, $6 and −$4. Efficiency retains positive-gain trades and rejects the negative one rather than maximizing quantity alone.

before.q: Which statement best limits competitive efficiency?
options: It requires equal CS and PS
It applies only at zero price
It proves WTP equals need
It depends on assumptions and does not settle distributional fairness
before.feedback: Competitive surplus maximization depends on the model’s assumptions and addresses efficiency; it does not by itself determine whether the distribution of gains is fair.

after.q: A competitive market allocates goods to the highest willingness to pay, but some users impose uncompensated disposal harm and low-income households receive few goods. Which assessment separates efficiency assumptions from equity?
options: Competition rules out unpriced harm, while unequal access alone proves that all trades reduce total surplus.
Correcting harm necessarily gives every household an equal share, so no separate equity judgment remains.
The highest willingness-to-pay rule establishes social efficiency regardless of external harm and income differences.
Unpriced harm can invalidate the private surplus benchmark; unequal access raises a distinct equity question even after that harm is corrected.
after.feedback: Private willingness to pay and cost omit the external harm. Internalizing that cost targets efficiency, while deciding whether the resulting distribution is fair is a separate judgment.

before.q: Buyer value is $52, seller cost $18, and price $45. How is surplus divided?
options: $7 to buyer and $27 to seller
$34 to each
$27 to buyer and $7 to seller
$45 to buyer and $18 to seller
before.feedback: Consumer surplus is $52 - $45 = $7 and producer surplus is $45 - $18 = $27, for total surplus of $34.

after.q: A buyer values a unit at $52, seller cost is $18 and price is $45. A proposal lowers price to $25 while the same trade occurs and uses $3 of real administrative resources. Which comparison is correct?
options: Buyer surplus rises from $7 to $27 and seller surplus falls from $27 to $7; gross total stays $34, but net total becomes $31 after administration.
Buyer surplus rises $20, so total surplus rises from $34 to $54 before administration.
Seller surplus falls $20, so total surplus falls from $34 to $14 before administration.
Buyer and seller surplus each become $27, so net total is $51.
after.feedback: At either price the unadjusted gain is $52−$18=$34. Price reallocates $20 between parties. Real administration uses $3, leaving $31 net.

before.q: A buyer values a good at $52 and the seller's cost is $18. If the market price falls from $45 to $25, what changes?
options: Total falls to $9
Buyer gets $27, seller gets $7, and total remains $34
Both get $34
Producer surplus is negative
before.feedback: At a $25 price, consumer surplus is $52 - $25 = $27 and producer surplus is $25 - $18 = $7. The $34 total gain from exchange is unchanged.

after.q: A buyer values a unit at $52 and seller cost is $18. Price falls from $45 to $25 with the same buyer and seller. A second proposed cut to $15 would leave the seller unwilling to produce and there is no subsidy. Which comparison is right?
options: Both cuts only redistribute surplus because price can never affect whether a trade occurs.
The first cut redistributes a $34 gain; the second prevents the trade and loses that $34 gain.
The first cut creates $20 of new total surplus; the second creates another $10 even without production.
The first cut loses $20 of total surplus; the second restores it by lowering consumer spending.
after.feedback: At $25 the seller still covers the $18 cost, so total gains remain $34. At $15 production is not privately viable without other support; if the trade disappears, its positive gain is lost.

before.q: Why is a producer-surplus loss not necessarily a social loss of equal size?
options: Producer surplus never matters
Consumer surplus always falls more
Some may be transferred to consumers or government
Social loss equals revenue
before.feedback: A loss of producer surplus can be partly or fully transferred to consumers or the government. Only surplus that disappears is a social loss.

after.q: A policy lowers producer surplus by $80, raises consumer surplus by $45 and generates $25 of government revenue. It uses no additional administrative resources. What is the social loss, and why is it not $80?
options: $80; producer-surplus losses are always identical to social losses.
$150; add every group’s change without signs.
$10; $70 of the producer loss appears as gains to consumers and government.
$0; any government revenue exactly offsets all private losses.
after.feedback: Total-surplus change is −$80+$45+$25=−$10. Transfers to other groups explain why the loss to one group is not the total social loss.

before.q: Why is a consumer-surplus gain not necessarily a social gain of equal size?
options: Consumer surplus never matters
Producer surplus always rises too
Social gain equals price
It may come from a transfer out of producer surplus
before.feedback: A gain in consumer surplus can come from a transfer out of producer surplus. Social gain depends on the net change in total surplus.

after.q: A policy raises consumer surplus by $90 and reduces producer surplus by $65, but requires a $40 government payment. With no other resource effects, which conclusion correctly counts taxpayers?
options: Net total surplus rises $25: ignore the government payment when adding private surplus.
Net total surplus rises $90 because the consumer gain alone measures the benefit.
Net total surplus falls $105 because consumer gains cannot count toward welfare.
Net total surplus falls $15: $90−$65−$40.
after.feedback: Consumers, producers and government must be included consistently. The government payment is a cost to taxpayers: 90−65−40=−15. The net loss remains after internal transfers cancel.

before.q: A buyer and seller complete a trade that creates $24 in total gains. A price change shifts $7 of surplus from the seller to the buyer while the trade still occurs. What is total surplus after the price change?
before.feedback: The price change redistributes $7 but does not alter the $24 gain from the completed trade.

after.q: A trade creates $24 of total gains. A price rule shifts $7 from seller to buyer without changing the trade, while enforcing the rule consumes $5 of real resources. Which result separates distribution from the resource effect?
options: The $7 changes the split, while net total surplus falls from $24 to $19 because of enforcement.
Net total surplus rises to $26 because the $7 transfer is a benefit and enforcement costs $5.
Net total surplus falls to $12 because both the transfer and enforcement are social losses.
Net total surplus stays $24 because both enforcement and the payment rule are transfers.
after.feedback: The buyer’s $7 gain is the seller’s $7 loss, canceling in the total. Enforcement uses $5 of resources, leaving $19.

before.q: Four possible trades have value-minus-cost gains of $18, $9, $2, and −$4. Which quantity maximizes total surplus?
options: 1 trade
3 trades
2 trades
4 trades
before.feedback: Complete the three trades with nonnegative gains and reject the trade that would reduce total surplus.

after.q: Four trades have marginal gains $18, $9, $2 and −$4. Policy A allows the efficient trades; Policy B requires all four. Both transfer $10 from sellers to buyers and use $3 of administration. Which net-surplus comparison follows?
options: A yields $36 and B $32; include the transfer as an extra social benefit.
A yields $26 and B $22; the common transfer cancels and the forced fourth trade accounts for the $4 difference.
Both yield $26 because administration and distribution are identical.
A yields $16 and B $12; subtract the transfer as a resource cost.
after.feedback: The efficient first three gains sum to $29. A uses $3, leaving $26. B also includes the −$4 trade, leaving $22 after administration.

before.q: A market maximizes total surplus but leaves nearly all gains with sellers. Best judgment?
options: It cannot be efficient
Consumer surplus must be negative
It may be efficient yet raise equity concerns
Total surplus must be zero
before.feedback: The market can maximize total surplus while distributing nearly all of the gains to sellers, so efficiency and equity can point to different concerns.

after.q: Two policies preserve the same trades and total production cost. Policy A leaves $90 of surplus with sellers and $10 with buyers. Policy B leaves $60 with sellers and $40 with buyers. Which conclusion follows from surplus accounting alone?
options: B yields more total surplus because buyers receive a larger share.
A yields more total surplus because sellers receive a larger share.
Both yield $100 of total surplus; choosing between distributions requires an equity criterion beyond the sum.
Neither can be efficient because the two groups do not receive equal shares.
after.feedback: The totals are 90+10=100 and 60+40=100. With production and allocation fixed, the difference is distribution rather than measured total efficiency.

before.q: A policy keeps buyer allocation and quantity unchanged but lowers total production cost. Total surplus:
options: Falls by the cost reduction
Is unchanged
Becomes equal to revenue
Rises by the cost reduction
before.feedback: If buyer allocation and quantity stay unchanged while production cost falls, the saved cost increases total surplus by the same amount.

after.q: A policy keeps the goods and buyer allocation unchanged, saves $12 in production resources, but requires $5 of new search effort. It also transfers $20 from buyers to sellers. What is the total-surplus change?
options: A $27 increase: add the transfer to the net resource saving.
A $13 decrease: subtract the transfer from the net resource saving.
A $12 increase: search effort has no resource value.
A $7 increase: count the $12 saving and $5 search cost, while the $20 transfer cancels.
after.feedback: The unchanged allocation preserves gross buyer value. Net resource use falls $12−$5=$7. The $20 payment affects the split of gains rather than their total.

before.q: A six-buyer, six-seller market for maker-fair booths has buyer values [46, 38, 31, 23, 14, 8], seller costs [7, 15, 24, 29, 37, 43], and a common price of $27. Units are allocated by value and cost. Which full accounting is correct?
options: 3 units trade; consumer surplus is $35, producer surplus is $34, and total surplus is $69
3 units trade; consumer surplus is $69, producer surplus is $0, and total surplus is $69
3 units trade; consumer surplus is $34, producer surplus is $35, and total surplus is $69
4 units trade; total surplus is $96
before.feedback: At $27, 3 buyers and 3 sellers participate. Their separate surpluses sum to $69.

after.q: 6 buyers each want one unit with values [54, 48, 42, 36, 30, 24]; 6 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [49, 53, 57, 61, 65, 69]. Values and costs are in dollars. A 1-unit allocation uses the cheapest 1 sellers but serves the lowest-value buyer instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 1 values. A reassignment would restore the highest-value allocation without changing output, using $27 of real administrative resources. Which comparison is correct?
options: Reassignment recovers $5 before administration; its net change is $-22, because the existing allocation creates no surplus.
Reassignment leaves surplus unchanged before administration; its net change is −$27, because quantity does not change.
Reassignment recovers $30 before administration; its net change is $3, so reassign.
Reassignment recovers $30 before administration; its net change is $57, because administrative resources add to social gains.
after.feedback: The efficient allocation yields $5. Replacing the marginal served buyer valued at $54 with the lowest-valued buyer at $24 loses $30, leaving $-25. Correcting allocation restores $30, but costs $27, for a net change of $3.

before.q: In the maker-fair booths market, the efficient allocation completes 3 trades. A coordinator forces one additional trade using the next-highest buyer value and next-lowest seller cost. What happens?
options: Total surplus rises by $6 because one more unit is exchanged
Consumer surplus falls by $29 while producer surplus rises by the same amount
Total surplus is unchanged because any completed exchange is mutually beneficial
Total surplus falls by $6 because the extra unit costs $29 but is valued at $23
before.feedback: The forced extra unit contributes $23 - $29 = -$6 to total surplus.

after.q: 6 buyers each want one unit with values [26, 32, 38, 44, 50, 56]; 6 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [49, 41, 57, 45, 53, 61]. Values and costs are in dollars. A 2-unit allocation uses the cheapest 2 sellers but serves the lowest-value buyer instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 2 values. A reassignment would restore the highest-value allocation without changing output, using $27 of real administrative resources. Which comparison is correct?
options: Reassignment recovers $20 before administration; its net change is $-7, because the existing allocation creates no surplus.
Reassignment leaves surplus unchanged before administration; its net change is −$27, because quantity does not change.
Reassignment recovers $24 before administration; its net change is $51, because administrative resources add to social gains.
Reassignment recovers $24 before administration; its net change is −$3, so retain the current allocation under these costs.
after.feedback: The efficient allocation yields $20. Replacing the marginal served buyer valued at $50 with the lowest-valued buyer at $26 loses $24, leaving $-4. Correcting allocation restores $24, but costs $27, for a net change of $-3.

before.q: A six-buyer, six-seller market for specialty lessons has buyer values [44, 36, 28, 21, 13, 6], seller costs [5, 12, 19, 27, 35, 41], and a common price of $25. Units are allocated by value and cost. Which full accounting is correct?
options: 3 units trade; consumer surplus is $33, producer surplus is $39, and total surplus is $72
3 units trade; consumer surplus is $39, producer surplus is $33, and total surplus is $72
3 units trade; consumer surplus is $72, producer surplus is $0, and total surplus is $72
4 units trade; total surplus is $97
before.feedback: At $25, 3 buyers and 3 sellers participate. Their separate surpluses sum to $72.

after.q: 6 buyers each want one unit with values [50, 44, 38, 32, 26, 20]; 6 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30]. Values and costs are in dollars. A planner ranks values from high to low and costs from low to high. It claims only 4 units can maximize total surplus because the next unit creates no extra gain. Which diagnosis gives the largest efficient quantity and correct surplus?
options: The largest efficient quantity is 5, with total surplus $100; stopping at 4 ties that surplus because the next trade has zero marginal gain.
The largest efficient quantity is 4, with total surplus $100; a zero-gain trade necessarily lowers surplus.
All 6 units are efficient, with total surplus $90; every completed trade adds positive gain.
The largest efficient quantity is 5, with total surplus $126; count the marginal payment as an extra social gain.
after.feedback: Ranked marginal gains are [40, 30, 20, 10, 0, -10]. The first 4 are positive and the next is zero; therefore 4 and 5 tie at $100, and 5 is the largest maximizer. Later negative-gain trades reduce surplus.

before.q: In the specialty-lessons market, three trades are efficient. The fourth buyer values a lesson at $21 and the fourth seller’s cost is $27. What is the strongest reason to reject a fourth trade?
options: It would transfer $6 from the buyer to the seller
It would reduce total surplus by $6
It would leave total surplus unchanged
It would increase total surplus by $48
before.feedback: The fourth unit contributes $21 − $27 = negative $6.

after.q: 6 buyers each want one unit with values [22, 28, 34, 40, 46, 52]; 6 sellers each can supply one with resource costs [35, 27, 43, 31, 39, 47]. Values and costs are in dollars. A 3-unit allocation uses the cheapest 3 sellers but serves the lowest-value buyer instead of the marginal buyer among the highest 3 values. A reassignment would restore the highest-value allocation without changing output, using $21 of real administrative resources. Which comparison is correct?
options: Reassignment recovers $45 before administration; its net change is $24, because the existing allocation creates no surplus.
Reassignment recovers $18 before administration; its net change is −$3, so retain the current allocation under these costs.
Reassignment leaves surplus unchanged before administration; its net change is −$21, because quantity does not change.

The original tax loses $40; A eliminates the loss by redistributing revenue and B leaves only $15 of loss.

Total surplus rises by $60

after.feedback: Subtract the common $20 resource cost from each willingness to pay: $80 versus $50. Income can affect willingness to pay, so a different equity criterion may support the lower-dollar-surplus allocation.

after.q: An efficient trade creates $40 of total surplus, split $2 to the buyer and $38 to the seller. A proposed transfer gives $15 from seller to buyer without changing production or use, but implementing it consumes $3 of real resources. Which assessment is correct?

The transfer itself destroys $15 of surplus, so net total surplus is $22.

Before administration the split becomes $17/$23 with the same $40 total; after the $3 resource cost, net total surplus is $37, so distribution improves by a chosen equity criterion at a measured efficiency cost.
after.feedback: The $15 payment redistributes the existing $40. The $3 administrative resource use reduces net total surplus to $37. Whether the distributional change is worth that cost requires an equity judgment.

Total surplus falls by $200; equity necessarily worsens
Total surplus is unchanged; its distribution cannot change

after.q: A rule reallocates $200 of existing surplus from one group to another without changing any trade. It adds $212 of total surplus because both the transfer and restored trade create new resources.
It reduces surplus by $188 because the transfer is a loss that offsets the new trade.
It adds $18 because the $6 real implementation cost does not affect surplus.
after.feedback: The original transfer leaves total surplus unchanged. The extra trade creates $18 of gains and uses $6 of implementation resources, adding $12 beyond that redistribution.

It equals income
It is seller marginal cost
It equalizes utility

after.q: A buyer’s maximum willingness to pay is $28. A seller offers the unit for $24, with no other costs. What is the buyer’s gain from accepting?

It is buyer value
It is the minimum compensation needed to cover opportunity cost
It excludes resource costs
