Accounting profit stays $60000, but economic profit becomes −$5000; the outside alternative now pays $5000 more.
Accounting profit stays $60000 and economic profit rises by $22000; a better outside offer increases the business return.
after.feedback: Accounting profit is $149000−$89000=$60000. The new opportunity cost is $57000+$8000; subtracting it gives −$5000. Positive accounting profit does not establish that the business beats the best alternative.

before.q: At Maple Street Media, output remains unchanged at Q = 26, an annual fixed fee adds $240 and the wage per worker rises $15. Productivity is unchanged. Which set of new cost values is correct?
before.feedback: Rebuild fixed and variable totals separately, divide by Q, and use the new wage over unchanged MP for MC.

after.q: At Maple Street Media, 3 workers each earn $100 per production period, and total fixed cost is $195 per period. The last worker raises output from 15 to 26 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
after.feedback: The new fixed cost is $435 and the wage bill is 3×$115=$345. Divide each by 26 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 11 units, so MC=$115/11=$10.45.

before.q: Granite Toolworks has revenue of $298,000, explicit costs of $188,000, a forgone salary of $60,000, and forgone capital income of $21,000. Which set of accounting profit, implicit cost, and economic profit is correct?
options: Accounting profit=$29,000; implicit cost=$188,000; economic profit=$110,000
Accounting profit=$110,000; implicit cost=$81,000; economic profit=$29,000
Accounting profit=$110,000; implicit cost=$60,000; economic profit=$50,000
Accounting profit=$217,000; implicit cost=$188,000; economic profit=$29,000
before.feedback: Compute recorded profit, total owner opportunity cost, and economic profit in sequence.

after.q: Granite Toolworks expects annual revenue of $298000, explicit costs of $188000, forgone salary of $60000, and forgone capital income of $21000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. For next year, revenue rises $20000, explicit costs rise $25000, and forgone capital income falls $10000; forgone salary is unchanged. Which comparison is correct?
options: Accounting and economic profit both fall $5000 because only explicit costs matter.
Accounting profit falls $5000, but economic profit rises $5000 to $34000.
Accounting profit rises $5000, while economic profit falls $5000 because capital income fell.
Accounting profit falls $15000 and economic profit falls $15000 because the lower outside return is an extra cost.
after.feedback: The business cash margin changes by +$20000−$25000=−$5000. The opportunity cost of capital falls $10000, so economic profit changes by −$5000+$10000=+$5000.

before.q: At Granite Toolworks, output remains unchanged at Q = 52, an annual fixed fee adds $240 and the wage per worker rises $15. Productivity is unchanged. Which set of new cost values is correct?
before.feedback: Rebuild fixed and variable totals separately, divide by Q, and use the new wage over unchanged MP for MC.

after.q: At Granite Toolworks, 4 workers each earn $145 per production period, and total fixed cost is $390 per period. The last worker raises output from 39 to 52 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
after.feedback: The new fixed cost is $630 and the wage bill is 4×$160=$640. Divide each by 52 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 13 units, so MC=$160/13=$12.31.

before.q: Lakeside Ceramics has revenue of $177,000, explicit costs of $109,000, a forgone salary of $40,000, and forgone capital income of $10,000. Which set of accounting profit, implicit cost, and economic profit is correct?
options: Accounting profit=$68,000; implicit cost=$50,000; economic profit=$18,000
Accounting profit=$18,000; implicit cost=$109,000; economic profit=$68,000
Accounting profit=$68,000; implicit cost=$40,000; economic profit=$28,000
Accounting profit=$127,000; implicit cost=$109,000; economic profit=$18,000
before.feedback: Compute recorded profit, total owner opportunity cost, and economic profit in sequence.

after.q: Lakeside Ceramics expects annual revenue of $177000, explicit costs of $109000, forgone salary of $40000, and forgone capital income of $10000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. A new technology would save $18000 in explicit costs but require owner capital that could earn an additional $25000 elsewhere. Revenue and forgone salary would not change. Which recommendation follows from the incremental comparison?
options: Retain the current technology: accounting profit would rise $18000, but economic profit would fall $7000.
Adopt the technology: accounting profit rises $18000, so economic profit must also rise $18000.
Adopt the technology: the additional $25000 forgone return is a benefit rather than a cost.
Retain the current technology because accounting profit would fall $7000 while economic profit rises.
after.feedback: Compare the $18000 explicit-cost saving with the $25000 added opportunity cost. The net economic change is −$7000, even though reported accounting profit would improve.

before.q: At Lakeside Ceramics, output remains unchanged at Q = 58, an annual fixed fee adds $240 and the wage per worker rises $15. Productivity is unchanged. Which set of new cost values is correct?
before.feedback: Rebuild fixed and variable totals separately, divide by Q, and use the new wage over unchanged MP for MC.

after.q: At Lakeside Ceramics, 5 workers each earn $115 per production period, and total fixed cost is $225 per period. The last worker raises output from 48 to 58 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
after.feedback: The new fixed cost is $465 and the wage bill is 5×$130=$650. Divide each by 58 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 10 units, so MC=$130/10=$13.00.

before.q: Prairie Solar has revenue of $329,000, explicit costs of $211,000, a forgone salary of $64,000, and forgone capital income of $24,000. Which set of accounting profit, implicit cost, and economic profit is correct?
options: Accounting profit=$30,000; implicit cost=$211,000; economic profit=$118,000
Accounting profit=$118,000; implicit cost=$64,000; economic profit=$54,000
Accounting profit=$241,000; implicit cost=$211,000; economic profit=$30,000
Accounting profit=$118,000; implicit cost=$88,000; economic profit=$30,000
before.feedback: Compute recorded profit, total owner opportunity cost, and economic profit in sequence.

after.q: Prairie Solar expects annual revenue of $329000, explicit costs of $211000, forgone salary of $64000, and forgone capital income of $24000. All comparisons use the same year and risk. What outside salary would make the owner indifferent between continuing and the best alternative, and what happens if the offer is $3000 above that salary?
options: Indifference salary $118000; an offer $3000 higher leaves the forgone capital return irrelevant.
Indifference salary $64000; an offer $3000 higher leaves economic profit equal to the original $30000.
Indifference salary $329000; an offer $3000 higher changes accounting profit but not opportunity cost.
Indifference salary $94000; an offer $3000 higher makes economic profit −$3000 while accounting profit stays $118000.
after.feedback: Set revenue−explicit costs−salary−forgone capital return equal to zero: salary=$329000−$211000−$24000=$94000. A $3000 higher offer makes continuing $3000 worse than the alternative without altering business accounting profit.

before.q: At Prairie Solar, output remains unchanged at Q = 85, an annual fixed fee adds $240 and the wage per worker rises $15. Productivity is unchanged. Which set of new cost values is correct?
before.feedback: Rebuild fixed and variable totals separately, divide by Q, and use the new wage over unchanged MP for MC.

after.q: At Prairie Solar, 6 workers each earn $155 per production period, and total fixed cost is $450 per period. The last worker raises output from 74 to 85 units; labor is the only variable input. A recurring fixed fee adds $240 per period and pay rises $15 per worker. Output, employment and productivity remain unchanged. Which new cost values are correct? Round final results to cents.
after.feedback: The new fixed cost is $690 and the wage bill is 6×$170=$1020. Divide each by 85 for AFC and AVC; ATC uses their unrounded sum. The last worker adds 11 units, so MC=$170/11=$15.45.

before.q: Why can economic profit be lower than accounting profit?
options: Economic profit subtracts opportunity costs of owner resources
It ignores fixed costs
It adds revenue twice
Accounting profit includes all implicit costs
before.feedback: Implicit opportunity costs create the gap.

after.q: A firm has $90,000 revenue, $60,000 explicit costs and $20,000 forgone owner income. What is economic profit?
after.feedback: Economic profit subtracts explicit and implicit costs: 90,000−60,000−20,000=$10,000.

before.q: Zero economic profit signals that owner resources earn:
options: Nothing
Their opportunity cost
Only explicit cost
Maximum monopoly profit
before.feedback: Normal profit keeps owner resources in their current use.

after.q: An owner earns $25,000 accounting profit and forgoes $25,000 in its best alternative use of time and capital. What does economic profit equal?
options: $25,000: forgone returns are ignored.
$0: the owner’s opportunity cost is covered.
−$25,000: the accounting return does not count.
$50,000: add the two returns.
after.feedback: Economic profit is accounting profit minus implicit opportunity cost: 25,000−25,000=0.

before.q: A firm asks how much cost rises when output expands slightly. Which measure is relevant?
options: Average fixed cost
Total fixed cost
Marginal cost
Accounting profit
before.feedback: Marginal analysis focuses on incremental changes.

after.q: Total cost is $200 at 10 units and $224 at 12 units. What is average marginal cost over those two additional units?
options: $24 per unit
$18.67 per unit
$12 per unit
$2 per unit
after.feedback: ΔTC/ΔQ=(224−200)/(12−10)=24/2=$12 per additional unit.

before.q: Why does MC below ATC lower ATC?
options: Fixed cost rises
Demand shifts
Revenue exceeds cost
The added unit costs less than the current average
before.feedback: A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down.

after.q: Producing 10 units costs $100. The eleventh unit adds $6. What happens to average total cost?
options: It rises to $10.60.
It stays at $10.
It falls to $6.
It falls to about $9.64.
after.feedback: New ATC=106/11≈$9.64. The added unit costs less than the original $10 average.

before.q: Which cost is irrelevant to the marginal cost of one more unit?
options: Additional materials
A fixed payment that does not change with output
Additional labor
A per-unit royalty
before.feedback: A cost that does not change has zero marginal contribution.

after.q: A workshop pays fixed rent of $500. One extra unit requires $8 of material and $4 of labor; rent is unchanged. What is that unit’s marginal cost?
after.feedback: Only the additional material and labor enter this marginal cost: 8+4=$12.

before.q: For a competitive firm considering a change in output, which cost curve measures the incremental production cost?
options: AFC
Marginal cost
TFC
Accounting profit
before.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional cost of producing more output and is the relevant cost measure for incremental output decisions.

after.q: A price-taking firm can sell one extra unit for $18; making it adds $14 to total cost. What is the marginal profit from that unit?
after.feedback: Marginal revenue minus marginal cost is 18−14=$4.

before.q: Why is marginal cost relevant to a competitive firm’s supply decision?
options: It measures total demand
It measures the additional resource cost of another unit
It equals consumer surplus
It is fixed at every output
before.feedback: Marginal cost measures the additional production cost of another unit and therefore helps determine whether expanding output is worthwhile at a given market price.

after.q: A firm can sell another unit for $16, but its marginal cost is $19. Holding other choices fixed, should it add that unit?
options: Yes; it would raise profit by $3.
No; it would lower profit by $3.
Yes; any positive revenue raises profit.
No; the full $19 is a profit loss regardless of revenue.
after.feedback: The extra unit changes profit by 16−19=−$3.

before.q: How does the general idea of opportunity cost carry into a firm’s production-cost analysis?
options: Opportunity cost is replaced by accounting profit
A firm counts only costs that change with output
Resources supplied by the owner are valued by the best alternative return sacrificed
Only purchased inputs have opportunity cost
before.feedback: The same next-best-alternative principle applies to labor, capital, land, and other resources used by a firm.

after.q: An owner uses a building that could instead earn $12,000 in annual rent. No rent check is paid by the owner’s business. What annual cost should economic analysis include?
options: $0 because no payment occurs
$12,000 explicit wage cost
$12,000 implicit opportunity cost
$24,000 because both uses count at once
after.feedback: Using the building sacrifices the $12,000 rental alternative even without a cash payment.

before.q: How does opportunity cost explain the difference between accounting profit and economic profit?
options: Economic profit ignores explicit expenses
The two measures differ only when fixed cost changes
Economic profit subtracts the forgone returns of owner-supplied resources
Accounting profit subtracts more opportunity costs than economic profit
before.feedback: Economic profit extends accounting profit by charging the firm for owner resources at their next-best use.

after.q: Accounting profit is $42,000 and the owner forgoes a $35,000 outside salary, with no other implicit costs. What is economic profit?
after.feedback: Subtract the forgone owner return: 42,000−35,000=$7,000.

before.q: Why is the vertical distance between TC and TVC constant in a standard short-run total-cost graph?
options: The distance equals TFC, which does not vary with output
The distance equals MC, which is constant
TVC and TC have different output units
The distance equals profit
before.feedback: Because TC = TFC + TVC, the fixed-cost amount separates the two curves at every output.

after.q: At one output TC is $160 and TVC is $100. At a higher output TVC is $145 while fixed cost is unchanged. What is TC at the higher output?
after.feedback: The first row gives TFC=160−100=60. Add the same $60 to the new TVC: 145+60=$205.

before.q: How does the fixed-cost concept connect to the downward slope of AFC?
options: TFC falls automatically as output rises
Variable cost is spread across fewer units
AFC is determined by marginal product only
The same TFC is spread across more units as output rises
before.feedback: AFC falls because the numerator stays fixed while the denominator grows.

after.q: Fixed cost is $120. Output rises from 10 to 15 units without changing fixed cost. What is the new AFC?
after.feedback: Spread $120 across 15 units: AFC=$8, down from $12.

before.q: How does the identity TC = TFC + TVC connect to ATC?
options: ATC excludes fixed cost
Dividing by Q gives ATC = AFC + AVC
Dividing by Q gives ATC = MC + AVC
ATC equals TC minus output
before.feedback: The average-cost identity follows directly from the total-cost identity.

after.q: At an output of 20, AFC is $3 and AVC is $7. What is ATC?
after.feedback: ATC=AFC+AVC=3+7=$10 per unit.

before.q: How does a below-average marginal cost affect ATC?
options: It leaves ATC unchanged by definition
It makes AFC rise
It pulls ATC downward
It pushes ATC upward
before.feedback: The marginal-versus-average rule applies to costs just as it does to other averages.

after.q: At 5 units total cost is $50. The sixth unit adds $16. What is ATC at 6 units?
after.feedback: Total cost becomes $66; 66/6=$11. The above-average added cost raises ATC.

before.q: A dominant firm bundles a product with a service that has few substitutes. From an elasticity perspective, how is bundling likely to affect demand for the bundle?
options: Make demand perfectly elastic
Reduce effective substitution and make bundle demand less elastic
Increase cross-price elasticity with rivals
Eliminate the need to consider price
before.commonError: assumes_bundling_always_increases_elasticity
before.feedback: Bundling can differentiate the offer and reduce easy comparison.

after.q: A product initially has few close substitutes. A 10% price increase reduces its quantity demanded by 4%. Later, several close substitutes become available; the same 10% price increase reduces quantity demanded by 16%. The comparison uses the same adjustment period, and income, tastes and the product’s necessity status are unchanged. A manager claims the larger response is merely a movement along demand and provides no evidence that responsiveness changed. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: Accept the claim: the ratios 0.4 and 1.6 describe movements along demand. Because the product itself is unchanged, responsiveness should be treated as constant despite the difference between those ratios.

Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 as close substitutes expand. Each price experiment moves along its own demand curve, while the comparison shows changed responsiveness across periods.
Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 because consumers have more time to adjust later. Equal experiment lengths do not constrain the time-horizon explanation for the larger response.

Reject the claim: elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6 because the product becomes more like a luxury. A larger observed response establishes changed necessity status despite the stated comparison controls.
after.feedback: Using the stated percentage responses, |Ed| changes from 4/10=0.4 to 16/10=1.6. Each price change causes movement along the demand curve applicable then. The different responsiveness across periods is consistent with the new substitutes; equal adjustment periods and unchanged necessity status rule out the other explanations.

before.q: A sugar tax causes consumers to switch to untaxed substitutes. What does this reveal about the elasticity of demand for the taxed product and the design of the tax?
options: Demand is elastic; a broader tax base can limit substitution
Demand is perfectly inelastic, so the tax failed
Supply elasticity alone caused substitution
The statutory payer should be changed
before.feedback: Close substitutes generate a strong demand response and can erode a narrow tax base.

after.q: A tax raises a drink’s price by 10% and reduces its quantity demanded by 18%, measured over the same period with other demand determinants held constant. Buyers switch to untaxed close substitutes. Which conclusion best connects the measured response to tax design?
options: Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); covering the close substitutes could reduce this substitution channel, but would not by itself determine the new tax revenue.
Demand is inelastic over the observed change (|Ed|=0.56); covering the close substitutes would necessarily lower tax revenue.
Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); changing the statutory payer would remove the substitution channel.
Demand is elastic over the observed change (|Ed|=1.8); covering the close substitutes would guarantee that quantity and tax revenue stay unchanged.
after.feedback: The stated quantity response divided by the price change is 18/10=1.8. Untaxed close substitutes offer an avoidance margin. Expanding coverage can limit that margin, but revenue still depends on the tax rate and remaining quantity response.

before.q: A farm quota reduces output. Under what demand condition can farm revenue rise?
options: Elastic demand
Perfectly elastic demand
Positive cross-price elasticity alone
Inelastic demand
before.feedback: With inelastic demand, the price rise dominates the quantity loss.

after.q: A farm quota reduces quantity 5% and raises price 8%, with no other change. A student says fewer sales must lower revenue. Which correction is right using the exact stated percentage changes?
options: Revenue falls 5% because the price increase does not affect revenue per sale.
Revenue rises exactly 13% because the magnitudes of both percentage changes should be added.
Revenue stays unchanged because all quota policies imply unit elasticity.
Revenue rises about 2.6% because 1.08×0.95=1.026; quantity falls proportionately less than price rises.
after.feedback: Revenue is price times quantity. The new revenue factor is 1.08×0.95=1.026, so revenue rises 2.6%; a lower quantity alone does not determine revenue.

before.q: A monopolist’s demand elasticity at the current output is 0.8. What does this reveal?
options: Demand is inelastic with negative marginal revenue
The firm is at maximum profit
Marginal revenue is positive
Demand is perfectly elastic
before.feedback: A profit-maximizing monopolist with positive marginal cost does not operate on inelastic demand.

after.q: A seller faces downward-sloping demand with absolute elasticity 0.8 at its current output. An analyst proposes a small output expansion to raise total revenue. Which response follows from elasticity, without needing a cost model?
options: Reject the revenue claim: the current range is inelastic, so marginal revenue is negative and a small output reduction raises revenue.
Accept the claim: any positive price makes marginal revenue positive regardless of elasticity.
Reject the claim because marginal revenue is zero whenever elasticity is below one.
Accept the claim because inelastic demand means quantity changes proportionately more than price.
after.feedback: In the inelastic range, expanding sales requires a proportionately large price reduction, reducing revenue. Thus MR is negative; the conclusion is about revenue rather than a complete profit choice.

before.q: Demand is Q = 120 − 3P. At P = 30, Q = 30. What is point elasticity?

after.q: Demand is Q=120−3P. Compare P=$30 with P=$10. Which statement explains why a constant slope does not imply constant point elasticity?
options: Both points have |Ed|=3 because the demand slope is −3, so revenue falls at both.
At $30, Q=30 and |Ed|=3; at $10, Q=90 and |Ed|=1/3, so a small price rise lowers revenue at the first point but raises it at the second.
At $30, |Ed|=1/3; at $10, |Ed|=3, so revenue effects are reversed.
Both points have unit elasticity because the demand equation is linear.
after.feedback: Point elasticity is |dQ/dP|×P/Q. It equals 3×30/30=3 at the high price and 3×10/90=1/3 at the low price. The P/Q ratio changes even though slope does not.

before.q: Supply is Q = 20 + 2P. At P = 20, Q = 60. What is point elasticity?
options: About 0.67

after.q: Supply is Q=20+2P. At P=$20, a planner uses the slope 2 as elasticity and forecasts a 20% quantity rise after a small 10% price increase. Which correction is correct?
options: Elasticity is 2 because slope and elasticity are equal for any straight line; the 20% forecast is correct.
Elasticity is 60/20=3; the quantity response is approximately 30%.
Elasticity is 2×20/60≈0.67; the approximate quantity response is 6.7%, not 20%.
Elasticity is 0.67, so quantity falls 6.7% when price rises.
after.feedback: At P=20, Q=60. Elasticity multiplies slope by P/Q: 2×20/60=2/3. The forecast quantity response is (2/3)×10%≈6.7%.

before.q: A rival price cut reduces a firm’s demand 15 percent. The rival price fell 10 percent. What is cross-price elasticity?
options: 1.5, indicating substitutes
−1.5, indicating complements
0.67, indicating substitutes
The relationship cannot be measured

after.q: A rival’s 10% price cut reduces a firm’s sales by 15%, with its own price held fixed. Using the resulting cross-price elasticity, what would a small 4% rival price increase predict, and what relationship is indicated?
options: About a 6% sales increase; the goods are substitutes because the cross-price elasticity is +1.5.
About a 6% sales decline; the goods are complements because the original sales change was negative.
About a 1.5% sales increase; elasticity is already a percentage forecast.
About a 2.7% sales increase; use the reciprocal of the observed response ratio.
after.feedback: The ratio is (−15%)/(−10%)=+1.5. A 4% rival-price rise predicts 1.5×4%=6% more sales, consistent with substitution.

before.q: Income falls 4 percent and demand for a product rises 6 percent. What is income elasticity and classification?
options: 1.5; normal good
−1.5; inferior good
−0.67; complement
0.67; normal good

after.q: Income falls 4% and product demand rises 6%, with prices and other determinants unchanged. If the estimated income elasticity applies to a subsequent small 2% income increase, what is the forecast and classification?
options: Demand rises about 3%; discard the negative sign when using income elasticity.
Demand falls about 3%; the good is inferior over the observed range.
Demand falls about 1.5%; the elasticity coefficient itself is the forecast percentage.
Demand rises about 8%; add the observed quantity change to the new income change.
after.feedback: Income elasticity is 6/(−4)=−1.5. Multiplying by the new +2% income change gives −3%. Its negative sign identifies an inferior good over this range.

before.q: A minimum wage raises employment costs by 10 percent in a market where the elasticity of labor demand is 1.4. What is the approximate percentage change in employment?
options: A 7.1 percent decline
A 14 percent increase
No effect because wages are not output prices
A 14 percent decline
before.feedback: 1.4 × 10% = 14% in the opposite direction.

after.q: A wage floor raises the wage employers pay by 10%. Estimated labor-demand elasticity is −1.4 in the short run and −2 in the long run. A forecast says employment must fall exactly 14% in both periods. Which correction follows under the stated fixed-demand-determinant estimates?
options: The approximate declines are 1.4% and 2%; elasticity coefficients already state total percentage changes.
Employment rises 14% and 20% because labor supply slopes upward.
Employment falls 14% in both periods because the same wage change implies the same quantity response.
The approximate declines are 14% and 20%; longer-run substitution makes the second response larger.
after.feedback: Multiply each elasticity by +10%: −14% and −20%. These are local approximations, not exact universal predictions, and different horizons need not share one elasticity.

before.q: Checkpoint: Using the two labeled points on vertical D2, what is the midpoint price elasticity of demand?
options: Undefined because price changes
before.feedback: Quantity is unchanged between the two points, so the percentage change in quantity is zero and PED equals zero.

after.q: Use the two labeled points on vertical D2. A student correctly computes zero midpoint demand elasticity, then concludes that total revenue is unchanged between the points. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Zero quantity change gives zero elasticity, but the higher-price point has higher revenue because the same positive quantity sells at a higher price.
Zero elasticity also means zero price change, so equal revenue follows.
Zero elasticity means quantity rises enough to offset the price rise, so equal revenue follows.
A vertical demand curve has infinite elasticity, so the midpoint calculation must be reversed.
after.feedback: For vertical D2, quantity is unchanged while price differs. The midpoint quantity-change numerator is zero. Revenue is P×Q, so with a positive fixed Q the higher price produces higher revenue.

before.q: A market’s demand becomes more elastic after information improves. What mechanism is most plausible?
options: Sellers lose all production capacity
Income elasticity becomes zero
Buyers can compare prices and substitutes more easily
The statutory tax payer changes
before.feedback: Information lowers search costs and supports substitution.

after.q: A price-comparison service makes close substitutes easier to find. Before its launch a 5% price increase reduced sales by 2%; afterwards the same increase reduces sales by 8%, over equal adjustment periods. Which interpretation and revenue prediction fit the evidence?
options: Absolute demand elasticity falls from 2.5 to 0.625; a small price increase now tends to raise revenue.
Demand becomes more elastic solely because the firm moves upward along an unchanged demand curve; comparison information plays no role.
Absolute demand elasticity rises from 0.4 to 1.6; a small price increase now tends to reduce revenue because buyers can switch more easily.
Demand remains inelastic because both tests use the same price increase; quantity responses cannot change the classification.
after.feedback: The response ratios are 2/5=0.4 and 8/5=1.6. Easier comparison improves substitution options. Above unit elasticity, the percentage quantity loss outweighs a small price increase.

before.q: A product’s demand is inelastic at current prices, but a close substitute is scheduled to launch. How should a long-term revenue forecast account for the substitute’s entry?
options: Let elasticity rise after substitute entry
Assume elasticity remains fixed forever
Set elasticity to zero after entry
Use supply elasticity as demand elasticity
before.feedback: Market structure changes can alter responsiveness.

after.q: A seller forecasts that a 5% price rise will raise revenue using today’s demand elasticity of 0.4. A close substitute launches before the planned price rise. Which revision and test would make the forecast more defensible?
options: Reestimate demand after entry; if elasticity rises above one, the predicted revenue effect can reverse.
Keep 0.4 because elasticity is a permanent property of the product; test only whether accounting costs changed.
Raise the revenue forecast automatically because a new substitute always increases demand for this seller’s product.
Use supply elasticity in place of demand elasticity because another producer has entered.
after.feedback: The new substitute changes buyers’ alternatives. The revenue prediction depends on responsiveness at the time of the price change, so an estimate above one can overturn the old inelastic-demand forecast.

before.q: Why can elasticity estimates differ across demographic groups even for the same product and price?
options: Substitutes, budget shares, preferences, and constraints differ across groups
Elasticity is a physical constant of the product
Different groups use different currencies
Only supply can vary across groups
before.feedback: Elasticity reflects choice context, not just product identity.

after.q: Two customer groups buy the same product at the same price. A 4% price increase reduces Group A’s purchases by 2% and Group B’s by 8%. Both groups have the same adjustment period. B spends a larger income share on the product and has more substitutes. Which conclusion is justified?
options: A is less responsive than B, consistent with the stated budget-share and substitution differences; equal prices do not imply equal elasticities.
A is more responsive than B because a smaller quantity response gives the larger elasticity.
Both have the same elasticity because price and adjustment period are the same; the responses measure supply instead.
The comparison proves that time horizon explains the difference, despite the identical adjustment periods.
after.feedback: The absolute elasticities are 0.5 and 2. Greater budget exposure and more substitutes are plausible reasons for B’s stronger response; the equal time horizon rules out that particular explanation.

options: Any zero observed change proves perfect inelasticity
Noise, contracts, and a tiny test may hide the response
Demand can respond only after a supply shift
Perfect inelasticity is the default
The zero response estimates elasticity precisely at zero; repeat the same tiny test only to check the seller’s revenue arithmetic.
The test may hide a response because of noise, contracts or its size; vary the test and allow adjustment before treating demand as perfectly inelastic.
The test establishes elastic demand because buyers delayed purchases; a larger increase must therefore raise revenue.
The test establishes unit elasticity because quantity was stable; the next test should hold total revenue constant.

before.q: A government publishes one national elasticity for housing. Why should local planners be cautious?
options: Elasticity is never useful for housing
National estimates are always perfectly elastic
Local land, regulation, vacancy, and time horizons differ
Only income elasticity matters locally
before.feedback: Housing responsiveness is highly context-dependent.

after.q: A national housing-supply estimate is 1.2 over ten years. City A has little buildable land and a one-year planning horizon; City B has available land and a ten-year horizon. Which use of the estimate is defensible?
options: Apply 1.2 to both cities because a national elasticity incorporates each local constraint equally.
Apply a larger elasticity to A because scarce land makes each price increase more valuable to owners.
Treat it as a starting point, not a common local forecast; A likely faces tighter short-run constraints, while B has more adjustment possibilities.
Apply zero elasticity to B because a longer horizon fixes the housing stock more tightly.
after.feedback: Supply responsiveness depends on available resources and adjustment time. A national long-horizon estimate cannot identify either city’s elasticity without local evidence, particularly A’s constrained short-run response.

options: Demand is definitively elastic
Demand is definitively inelastic
Price should be doubled immediately
The revenue effect is uncertain and calls for cautious testing
The price increase should lower revenue because the point estimate exceeds one; the interval affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
The price increase should raise revenue because the interval includes inelastic values; the point estimate affects the size but cannot affect the sign.
Revenue should be unchanged because the interval includes one; averaging elastic and inelastic estimates guarantees unit elasticity.
The revenue effect of a small price change is uncertain because plausible elasticity values fall on both sides of one; use cautious testing.
Brand demand can be elastic even when category demand is inelastic
Necessity guarantees every brand is inelastic
Brand and category elasticity must be identical
Supply elasticity determines brand demand
Brand demand can be elastic even if category demand is inelastic, because consumers can switch brands without giving up the necessity.
Brand demand should be less elastic than category demand, because a brand includes fewer possible purchases than the category.
Brand and category demand should have equal elasticity, because both purchases satisfy the same basic need.
Brand demand can be elastic only if the entire category is a luxury, because generic substitutes cannot change necessity status.
Demand must be perfectly inelastic
The opposing determinants make direct estimation necessary
Demand must be perfectly elastic
Budget share never matters without substitutes
Few substitutes establish inelastic demand; budget share changes spending levels but cannot affect responsiveness.
Few substitutes restrain responsiveness while a large budget share encourages adjustment; estimate their combined effect in this market.
The large budget share establishes elastic demand; the absence of substitutes changes price but cannot affect responsiveness.
The two determinants imply unit elasticity; their opposing directions necessarily cancel quantitatively.
Burden can never change after enactment
Long-run burden shifts entirely to sellers
Tax incidence depends only on the first-year statute
Long-run burden may shift toward the demand side as supply becomes more elastic
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to sellers.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, supply adjustment raises the quantity traded but leaves the burden shares at their short-run values.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, producers’ ability to adjust makes the statutory taxpayer bear a larger share over time.
If demand responsiveness is unchanged, the more elastic long-run supply tends to shift more of the burden to buyers.

before.q: A farm-support program wants to raise producer revenue by restricting output. When is the policy most likely to raise total farm revenue?
options: When demand is highly elastic
When demand for the crop is inelastic
When supply is perfectly elastic
When income elasticity is negative
before.feedback: With inelastic demand, the price rise from lower output can outweigh the quantity reduction.

after.q: A crop quota reduces sales from 1,000 to 900 units and raises price from $10 to $12. Farmers’ variable production cost falls by $300, while administering the quota uses $1,200 of their resources. Which comparison avoids confusing revenue with profit?
options: Revenue rises by $800 and profit must rise by $800 because the demand response is inelastic.
Revenue rises by $800, but net producer profit falls by $100 after cost savings and administration.
Revenue falls by $1,000 and profit falls by $1,900 because fewer units are sold.
Revenue rises by $1,200 and profit rises by $300 because use the old quantity at the new price.
after.feedback: Revenue changes from $10,000 to $10,800. Profit changes by +800+300−1,200=−$100. Inelastic response can raise revenue without making an administratively costly policy profitable.

options: Elastic demand means price can never rise
Elasticity guarantees profit falls with price
Profit also depends on margin and cost, so a higher price can still be optimal
Costs shift demand rather than supply
Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, so profit must fall by the same amount even if the firm avoids variable costs.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue gain from a price rise, and that gain is sufficient to establish a profit gain after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts a revenue loss from a price rise, but reduced unit sales and higher contribution margins may improve profit after the cost increase.
Elastic demand predicts unchanged revenue from a price rise, so the cost increase can be passed on without checking the quantity response.

before.q: A firm offers a lower price to customers with more elastic demand. Which condition is essential for the strategy to increase profit?
options: The elastic group must have higher willingness to pay
Both groups must face identical prices
Marginal cost must be zero
The firm must limit resale or switching between customer groups
before.feedback: Segmentation fails if buyers can arbitrage the price difference.

after.q: A seller expects a small discount to increase revenue from customers with elastic demand. Those customers can freely resell purchases to customers currently paying the regular price. Which issue must the forecast address before treating the two groups’ sales as separate?
options: Resale guarantees the discount raises profit because every discounted sale is an additional market sale.
Resale makes both groups’ demand perfectly inelastic because the seller names two prices.
Resale affects fixed cost only, so it can be ignored when estimating demand responses.
Resale can shift regular-price purchases into the discounted channel; evaluate that switching as well as each group’s quantity response.
after.feedback: The elastic group may buy partly for resale, replacing rather than adding to regular-price sales. Separate response estimates do not by themselves establish the seller’s overall revenue or profit gain.

before.q: A country’s demand for foreign currency is derived from import demand. If import demand becomes more elastic, foreign-currency demand is likely to:
options: Become more elastic
Become perfectly inelastic
Become unrelated to import prices
Turn negative at all exchange rates
before.feedback: More responsive import purchases make currency demand more responsive to its effective price.

after.q: An importer initially cuts foreign-goods purchases by 2% when their domestic-currency price rises 5%. After close domestic substitutes appear, the same price increase cuts imports 9%. If foreign prices and currency needed per imported unit are unchanged, which implication follows?
options: Import demand becomes more elastic, so the derived quantity demand for foreign currency becomes more responsive to the same domestic-currency price change.
Import demand becomes less elastic because 9% is larger than 2%, so foreign-currency purchases become less responsive.
The foreign-currency quantity must rise when imports fall, because each imported unit now requires more foreign currency.
Derived demand is unchanged because domestic substitutes cannot affect purchases of foreign goods.
after.feedback: The import response ratio rises from 0.4 to 1.8. With unchanged foreign currency required per unit, a larger percentage fall in imports produces a larger fall in currency purchases.

before.q: A retailer wants to forecast how a rival’s price promotion affects its own sales. Which elasticity is directly relevant?
options: Price elasticity of supply
Cross-price elasticity of demand
Income elasticity only
The rival’s total-revenue elasticity
before.feedback: Cross-price elasticity measures demand response to another product’s price.

after.q: A rival cuts its price 10%. Your product’s cross-price elasticity with that rival is +1.5, while your own-price elasticity is −0.5. Holding your price and other determinants fixed, which forecast and interpretation fit?
options: Your sales rise about 15%; positive cross-price elasticity means the goods are complements.
Your sales fall about 15%; the positive cross-price elasticity indicates substitutes.
Your sales rise about 5%; use own-price elasticity with the rival’s price cut.
Your sales fall about 0.15%; multiply by the elasticity as though it were already a percentage.
after.feedback: Use the cross-price coefficient for a rival’s price: 1.5×(−10%)=−15%. The positive relationship between rival price and own sales is the substitute pattern.

before.q: A government forecasts how income growth changes demand for public transit. Which elasticity is directly relevant?
options: Cross-price elasticity
Price elasticity of supply
Income elasticity of demand
Tax incidence elasticity
before.feedback: Income elasticity links demand to income changes.

after.q: Income is forecast to rise 5%. Transit demand has income elasticity −0.6; leisure-rail demand has income elasticity +1.4. Prices and other determinants are fixed. Which forecast separates the sign from responsiveness?
options: Transit demand rises about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; discard the minus sign before forecasting.
Transit demand falls about 0.6%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 1.4%; coefficients are percentage changes themselves.
Transit demand falls about 3%, while leisure-rail demand rises about 7%; the estimates classify transit as inferior over this range.
Both demands rise 5% because the income shock is common to the two markets.
after.feedback: Multiply each coefficient by the 5% income rise: −0.6×5%=−3% and 1.4×5%=7%. For income elasticity, the sign identifies the direction and must be retained.

before.q: A firm wants to predict how much quantity supplied will change when the price it receives for its product changes. Which elasticity is directly relevant?
options: Income elasticity of demand
Cross-price elasticity
Demand elasticity for a complement
Price elasticity of supply
before.feedback: Supply elasticity measures producer quantity response to the output price.

after.q: A producer’s price rises 8%. Its short-run supply elasticity is 0.25 and its long-run elasticity is 1.5, each applicable near the initial price. Which forecast and explanation fit, with other determinants held constant?
options: Quantity supplied rises 12% in the short run and 2% in the long run because time reduces adjustment options.
Quantity supplied rises 8% in both periods because elasticity measures the direction but not the size of the response.
Quantity supplied falls 2% then 12% because the higher output price raises the firm’s input costs by definition.
Quantity supplied rises about 2% in the short run and 12% in the long run as capacity and inputs can adjust.
after.feedback: Supply response is elasticity times the price change: 0.25×8%=2% and 1.5×8%=12%. Longer adjustment time can allow greater output response.

before.q: A researcher reports price elasticity of demand as −2.3 and another reports 2.3 for the same estimate. Are they necessarily inconsistent?
options: No; one reports the signed estimate and one its absolute value
Yes; elasticity can never be negative in any form
Yes; the positive value must be supply elasticity
No; the sign identifies an inferior good
before.feedback: Demand estimates are negative by the law of demand, but classifications commonly use absolute magnitude.

after.q: Two reports describe the same demand estimate as −2.3 and 2.3. A manager says they predict opposite sales responses to a 2% price increase. Which diagnosis is appropriate if the second report uses the absolute-value convention?
options: Both imply an approximate 4.6% sales decline; the second reports magnitude rather than an upward-sloping demand response.
One predicts a 4.6% decline and the other a 4.6% rise because absolute values reverse economic behavior.
Both predict a 2.3% sales decline because elasticity should not be multiplied by the price change.
Neither permits a revenue prediction because opposite printed signs prove the data disagree.
after.feedback: The signed estimate gives −2.3×2%=−4.6%. Reporting |Ed|=2.3 retains that downward-demand interpretation; it changes notation, not the estimated behavior.

before.q: A researcher reports cross-price elasticity of −0.9. Should the sign be discarded?
options: Yes; only magnitude matters
Yes; negative values are calculation errors
No; it indicates the goods are complements
No; it indicates both goods are inferior
before.feedback: The sign distinguishes complements from substitutes.

after.q: A product has cross-price elasticity −0.9 with a companion service. The service price falls 10%. An analyst discards the minus sign and forecasts a 9% product-sales decline. Which correction is right?
options: Discard the sign: product sales fall about 9%, consistent with the purchases being substitutes.
Keep the sign: product sales fall about 0.9%, because the coefficient already contains the 10% price change.
Keep the sign: product sales rise about 9%, consistent with the two purchases being complements.
Discard both signs: product sales are unchanged because cross-price elasticity cannot predict quantity.
after.feedback: For cross-price elasticity the sign distinguishes complements from substitutes. (−0.9)×(−10%)=+9%, so a cheaper complement raises demand for the product.

before.q: A government combines a tax, a binding price ceiling, and a subsidy for approved buyers in one market. What is the sound first step in elasticity analysis?
options: Add all statutory rates and assign the sum to sellers
Use demand elasticity alone for every effect
Assume the policies cancel because some raise and some lower price
Separate the policy wedges before analyzing curves, prices, and incidence
before.feedback: Layered policies must be decomposed before relative elasticities can be applied.

after.q: A binding posted-price ceiling holds the seller’s receipt at $10. Buyers must also pay a $2 per-unit tax, and approved buyers receive a $1 per-unit subsidy. Supply at the ceiling is only 60 units while buyers seek 100. Which analysis correctly distinguishes prices from actual trades?
options: Approved buyers pay $9 and sellers receive $12; all 100 desired units trade because the subsidy removes scarcity.
Approved buyers pay $13 and sellers receive $10; trades are 100 because all policy amounts should be added to demand.
Approved buyers pay $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are necessarily 100 because those prices clear any market.
Approved buyers’ net monetary outlay is $11 and sellers receive $10; trades are limited to 60, so a demand-elasticity calculation alone cannot establish 100 sales.
after.feedback: For approved buyers, $10+$2−$1=$11. Sellers still receive the capped $10, at which only 60 units are supplied. The binding shortage constrains actual trades regardless of desired purchases.

options: Because optimal pricing must account for elasticity together with marginal cost and capacity constraints
Elasticity is irrelevant whenever capacity exists
The most elastic group should always receive the highest price
All customers must be charged marginal cost
A lower price may attract more units from responsive customers, but those units use scarce capacity and may carry rising marginal cost; compare incremental contribution across feasible uses.
A lower price attracts more units from responsive customers, so allocate all capacity to them even when their incremental contribution is lower.
Rising marginal cost changes total profit but not the contribution of extra units, so allocate capacity using elasticity alone.
A capacity limit makes demand responses irrelevant until capacity expands, so allocate current capacity only by customers’ average spending.

before.q: Demand for a product is less elastic than supply. Which concept uses this difference in elasticity to determine who bears more of a tax?
options: Comparative advantage
GDP measurement
Economic tax incidence
Money creation
before.feedback: Relative elasticity determines economic tax incidence.

after.q: Demand elasticity has magnitude 0.3 and supply elasticity is 1.2 in a competitive market. Which side bears more of a small per-unit tax?
options: Sellers, because supply is more elastic.
Both equally, because the tax is per unit.
Buyers, because demand is less elastic.
The side legally sending the payment, regardless of elasticity.
after.feedback: Buyers adjust quantity less readily than sellers; the less elastic side bears more of the tax.

before.q: A tax creates a larger quantity reduction in a highly elastic market. Which concept measures the resulting lost gains from trade?
options: Income inequality only
Nominal GDP
Money neutrality
Deadweight loss
before.feedback: The lost trades create deadweight loss.

after.q: Two competitive markets receive the same $4 per-unit tax and have linear curves with no other distortions. Quantity falls by 10 units in A and 30 in B. Which has the greater deadweight loss?
options: A: $40 versus B: $120
Both: $4
B: $120 versus A: $40
B: $60 versus A: $20
after.feedback: DWL is half the tax wedge times lost quantity: A=0.5×4×10=$20 and B=0.5×4×30=$60.

before.q: A wage increase changes employment. Which area of microeconomics applies elasticity to the demand for inputs such as labor?
options: Public goods
Consumer choice only
Perfect competition in money markets
Factor markets
before.feedback: Labor demand is a derived factor demand.

after.q: Labor-demand elasticity is −0.8. With other conditions fixed, use the small-change approximation to predict employment after a 5% wage increase.
options: Employment rises about 4%.
Employment falls about 6.25%.
Employment rises about 5%.
Employment falls about 4%.
after.feedback: Percentage employment change is −0.8×5%=−4%; labor is the input demanded.

before.q: An emissions tax changes output. Which concept explains why a corrective tax may be justified in the first place?
options: Externalities
Monetary neutrality
Income effects only
Comparative advantage
before.feedback: The external cost motivates correction; elasticity predicts response.

after.q: A factory’s output imposes an unpriced $3 external cost per unit. A corrective tax raises its relevant per-unit cost, and output demand is price-responsive. Which outcome is consistent with the purpose of the tax?
options: Output falls as the firm faces more of the social cost of production.
Output rises because an external cost is an extra benefit.
The tax is justified only if output cannot change.
The external cost disappears solely because tax revenue is collected.
after.feedback: The unpriced harm motivates correction; incorporating that cost can reduce output and associated harm. Revenue collection itself is not removal of the physical externality.

before.q: How does the total-revenue formula connect a demand curve to firm revenue?
options: The demand slope directly equals total revenue
Revenue is the area above demand and below price
Quantity alone determines revenue
Each price-quantity point implies revenue equal to P × Q
before.commonError: needs_targeted_recovery
before.feedback: A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue.

after.q: A demand point has price $12 and quantity 50. What is total revenue at that point?
after.feedback: Multiply price by units sold: $12×50=$600.

before.commonError: needs_targeted_recovery
needs_targeted_recovery

before.q: How does elasticity connect to marginal-revenue reasoning for a firm with downward-sloping demand?
options: MR is positive on the elastic portion and negative on the inelastic portion
MR is always zero when price changes
Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than MR
MR is positive only when demand is perfectly inelastic
before.commonError: needs_targeted_recovery
before.feedback: The elasticity region helps identify the sign of marginal revenue.

after.q: A seller is on a smooth downward-sloping demand segment with |Ed|=2. Is selling a little more output associated with positive or negative marginal revenue?
options: Positive: the quantity gain outweighs the price reduction’s effect on revenue.
Negative: every price reduction lowers total revenue.
Zero: every point on demand maximizes revenue.
Negative: elastic demand means quantity barely responds.
after.feedback: On an elastic segment, a small price reduction raises total revenue, so the extra output has positive MR.

before.commonError: needs_targeted_recovery

before.q: A seller receives $18 per unit and sells 400 units after a market change. Which measure combines these two values when evaluating the revenue effect?
options: Producer surplus always equals total revenue
Cross-price elasticity equals $18 × 400
Total revenue equals the price received times quantity sold
Consumer surplus equals price times quantity
before.commonError: needs_targeted_recovery
before.feedback: Elasticity analysis often evaluates how price and quantity changes combine to change revenue.

after.q: A seller receives $18 per unit and sells 400 units after a change. What is its total revenue?
after.feedback: Total revenue is 18×400=$7,200, regardless of costs.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Suppose the wage is $30 per hour. What imbalance is visible in this warehouse labor market?
options: Labor demanded exceeds labor supplied
The market remains at equilibrium
Labor supplied exceeds labor demanded
Both curves shift right
before.feedback: At $30, the supply curve lies to the right of demand, so more workers seek jobs than firms wish to hire.

after.q: The graph’s competitive equilibrium is $20 per hour. A binding wage floor holds wages at $30, where labor supplied exceeds labor demanded. If the floor is removed with both curves unchanged, which adjustment is consistent with the model?
options: The wage falls toward $20; labor demand shifts right and labor supply shifts left solely because the wage falls.
The wage rises above $30; excess labor supply indicates employers cannot recruit enough workers.
The wage falls toward $20; labor demanded rises and labor supplied falls along their existing curves.
The wage stays at $30; removing the floor changes only the label attached to unemployment.
after.feedback: At the enforced above-equilibrium wage there is excess labor supply. Removing it permits a lower wage, increasing hiring and reducing the quantity offered along unchanged curves until they meet.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. If employment is 6,000 workers on the graph, what does the market wage imply?
options: The market is at the marked equilibrium
The displayed supply wage exceeds the displayed demand wage
Firms want more labor than workers supply
Labor demand must shift right
before.feedback: At 6,000 workers, the supply curve is above the demand curve. The wage workers require exceeds what firms are willing to pay for that quantity.

after.q: At 6,000 workers in the graph, the wage required by labor supply exceeds firms’ marginal willingness to pay on labor demand. A proposal forces hiring up to that level without changing productivity or workers’ opportunity costs. Which marginal assessment is correct?
options: Every extra wage dollar is a net social gain, so hiring beyond the demand-supply intersection must raise surplus.
Some additional hires have opportunity cost above their marginal product value; wage payments alone do not establish a net social gain.
Marginal product value exceeds opportunity cost because labor supply lies above demand at 6,000.
No marginal comparison is possible because labor demand measures average rather than marginal product value.
after.feedback: Labor supply reflects workers’ marginal opportunity cost and demand their marginal product value in this competitive model. When supply lies above demand, forcing those extra hires uses resources worth more than the output they add.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. How does the demand increase change the warehouse labor market?
options: The wage rises and employment falls
The wage falls and employment rises
Both the wage and employment fall
Both the equilibrium wage and employment rise
before.feedback: The equilibrium moves from 4,000 workers at $20 to 6,000 at $25, so both market outcomes rise.

after.q: The graph moves from 4,000 warehouse workers at $20 to 6,000 at $25 with labor supply unchanged. A manager attributes the increase to more workers becoming available at every wage. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The manager is correct because any rise in employment must be a rightward labor-supply shift.
The graph shows movement down unchanged labor demand because the wage rose.
The graph shows lower labor demand because higher wages reduce firms’ desired employment at every wage.
The graph instead shows greater labor demand; employment rises despite a higher wage, while a supply expansion alone would tend to lower the wage.
after.feedback: The new outcome has both higher wage and employment and is on the unchanged supply curve. A rightward demand shift accounts for both; a supply expansion alone has a different wage direction.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. A new sorting system raises each warehouse worker's productivity. Which curve change in the graph fits that story?
options: Labor supply shifts left
There is movement down D L0
Labor demand shifts from D L0 to D L1
Both curves shift left
before.feedback: Higher worker productivity raises the value firms obtain from labor at each wage, matching the rightward demand shift shown.

after.q: The graph shows warehouse labor demand increasing. Suppose a sorting system raises marginal product by 25% at every employment level, but the competitive output price simultaneously falls by 10%. How does value of marginal product compare with its original level, and does that support the depicted demand shift?
options: It rises by 15%, supporting a rightward shift because the percentage changes should simply be subtracted.
It falls by 10%, contradicting the shift because product price alone determines labor demand.
It rises by 12.5%, supporting a rightward demand shift because 1.25×0.90=1.125.
It remains unchanged because a productivity gain and a price decline always cancel.
after.feedback: VMP is product price times marginal product. Combining the two changes gives 1.25×0.90=1.125, a 12.5% increase at each employment level, supporting increased labor demand.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Which part of the graph shows that this is a shift rather than movement along labor demand?
options: The wage axis is vertical
Two demand curves appear while labor supply is unchanged
The new equilibrium has a dot
The supply curve slopes upward
before.feedback: D L0 and D L1 show different quantities demanded at a given wage. That is a change in demand, not movement on one curve.

after.q: The graph shows D L0 shifting to D L1 while labor supply stays fixed. A report says “the higher wage caused labor demand to increase.” Which sequence correctly separates cause from movement?
options: The higher wage shifts labor demand right; the extra employment then shifts labor supply left.
An increase in productivity or output demand raises labor demand; the resulting higher wage brings movement along unchanged labor supply.
The higher wage moves employers down their original demand curve; no demand shifter is required.
Labor supply shifts right first; the higher wage is the normal result of that supply expansion.
after.feedback: A wage change moves quantity demanded along a labor-demand curve; it does not shift that curve. A demand determinant changes first, and the new equilibrium includes movement along supply.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. A disease reduces each orchard worker's harvest. How does the graph translate that productivity loss?
options: Lower productivity shifts labor supply left
The wage change alone shifts demand
Employment rises at every wage
Lower productivity shifts labor demand left
before.feedback: With less output per worker, the value of marginal product falls at each employment level, reducing labor demand.

after.q: A disease reduces each orchard worker’s marginal product by 20%, but the fruit price rises by 25%. Assume competitive output pricing and the same percentage productivity effect at each employment level. Does the graph’s leftward labor-demand shift necessarily follow after both changes?
options: Yes; a productivity decline shifts labor demand left regardless of product price.
No; VMP rises by 5% because the percentage changes should be added algebraically.
Yes; the fruit-price rise lowers VMP by increasing workers’ opportunity cost.
No; VMP is unchanged because 0.80×1.25=1, so the productivity loss alone does not determine the combined labor-demand effect.
after.feedback: Derived demand depends on price times marginal product. The stated price rise exactly offsets the productivity decline: 1.25×0.80=1. Neither effect can be considered alone.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Why does 40 on the horizontal axis not mean 40 warehouse workers?
options: The axis is measured in thousands, so 40 represents 40,000
The axis is measured in hundreds, so 40 represents 4,000
The wage axis supplies the missing zero
Only the curve labels determine employment
before.feedback: The horizontal-axis title explicitly uses hundreds of workers. Multiplying 40 by 100 gives 4,000 workers.

after.q: The graph marks employment at 40 on an axis measured in hundreds, with wage $20. A later equilibrium is 60 on the same scale at wage $25. An analyst reports payroll rises from $800 to $1,500, a 50% increase. Which correction is complete?
options: Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, a 50% increase because only employment matters.
Payroll rises from $80,000 to $150,000, an 87.5% increase; both the axis scale and the wage change matter.
Payroll rises from $800 to $1,500, an 87.5% increase because the axis scale does not affect dollar totals.
Payroll rises from $80,000 to $100,000, a 25% increase because the wage change alone determines payroll.
after.feedback: Employment is 4,000 then 6,000. Payrolls are 4,000×20=$80,000 and 6,000×25=$150,000. The gain is 70,000/80,000=87.5%, combining price and quantity changes.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. How large is the fall in orchard employment?
options: 200 workers
2,000 workers
4,000 workers
6,000 workers
before.feedback: Employment declines from 4,000 to 2,000 workers, a reduction of 2,000.

after.q: The orchard graph shows employment falling from 4,000 to 2,000 after a productivity loss at unchanged output price. A later output-price increase raises marginal revenue product, but its size is not given. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: The first employment loss is 2,000; any later price rise necessarily restores exactly 4,000 workers.
The first employment loss is 2,000; the later price rise partly offsets the demand reduction, but the final employment level relative to 4,000 is not determined.
The first employment loss is 200; a higher output price shifts labor supply right rather than demand.
The first employment loss is 4,000; the later price rise cannot affect derived labor demand.
after.feedback: Read the initial change with the hundreds-of-workers scale: 4,000−2,000=2,000. A higher output price raises product value per worker, opposing the original demand loss. Without the magnitude, restoration to or beyond the original level is uncertain.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Expanded nursing programs graduate more workers. Why is that a supply shift rather than movement along supply?
options: The equilibrium wage changes
The number of qualified workers changes at every wage
Labor demand slopes downward
Hospitals use derived demand
before.feedback: Training expands the qualified workforce, altering labor supplied at a given wage and shifting the entire curve.

after.q: Expanded nursing programs shift labor supply right as shown, from 4,000 nurses at $20 to 6,000 at $15. Hospitals then experience an increase in demand for care. With the size of that second shift unknown, which final comparison with the original equilibrium is justified?
options: Employment is higher and the wage must remain below $20 because the supply shift occurred first.
Employment is higher, but the wage can be below, equal to or above $20 because the supply and demand shifts have opposing wage effects.
Employment is lower and the wage must exceed $20 because demand shifts always reduce hiring.
Employment returns to 4,000 and the wage returns to $20 because two rightward shifts cancel.
after.feedback: More qualified workers and greater derived labor demand both support higher employment. Supply expansion tends to lower wages while demand expansion tends to raise them, so their relative strengths determine the final wage.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. At the $20 wage floor, how many restaurant workers do firms want to hire?
options: 200 workers
2,000 workers
4,000 workers
6,000 workers
before.feedback: The wage-floor line meets labor demand at 20 hundreds of workers, or 2,000 workers.

after.q: The restaurant graph shows an unregulated equilibrium of 4,000 workers at $15. At a $20 wage floor, firms demand 2,000 workers and 6,000 seek work. A report calls all 4,000 excess job seekers “jobs lost.” Which correction is right?
options: Jobs fall by 4,000 and excess labor supplied is 2,000 because both compare demand with the original employment level.
Jobs fall by 2,000, while excess labor supplied is 4,000; the latter includes additional workers attracted by the higher wage.
Jobs rise by 2,000 because labor supplied rises from 4,000 to 6,000.
Jobs remain 4,000 because a legal wage changes pay but not hiring.
after.feedback: Employment falls from 4,000 to 2,000, a 2,000-job decline. Excess supply at the floor is 6,000−2,000=4,000; that differs from the fall in jobs.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. What competitive outcome is shown for the nursing market?
options: 4,000 nurses at $20 per hour
6,000 nurses at $25 per hour
4,000 nurses at $30 per hour
8,000 nurses at $25 per hour
before.feedback: Labor supply intersects MRP at 60 hundreds of nurses and $25 per hour, the competitive benchmark.

after.feedback: Compare added revenue with the $100 wage. 22×$6=$132 exceeds the wage; 14×$6=$84 does not. Diminishing marginal product need not mean negative marginal product or immediate unprofitability.

after.q: A hypothetical poverty measure counts cash income but excludes food vouchers. A household has $25,000 in cash and $3,000 in vouchers; its threshold is $27,000. Replacing the vouchers with $3,000 cash changes no prices. Which conclusion follows?
options: Measured status remains below because transfers never enter cash income.
Measured status changes from above to below because vouchers are counted twice.
Measured status remains above because the original vouchers already count as cash.
Measured status changes from below to above the threshold, though this alone does not measure the change in well-being.
after.feedback: The measure initially counts $25,000 and then $28,000. Classification changes mechanically; the economic value of relaxing spending restrictions is a separate question.

before.q: Data for hypothetical Economy P show that the official threshold for a household is $31,000 and measured money income is $32,800. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
options: Below the threshold because every household is poor
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
Above the poverty threshold
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Poverty Thresholds and Measurement.
before.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $32,800, with the $31,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

after.q: Two households each have $31,000 measured income. The threshold is $30,000 for the smaller household and $34,000 for the larger. An analyst classifies both as above poverty because their incomes match. What is the error?
options: The analyst should classify both below poverty because their incomes match.
The analyst should compare the smaller household with the larger household’s threshold only.
The analyst should average the thresholds before classifying either household.
The analyst ignores different applicable thresholds; only the smaller household is above its threshold.
after.feedback: Each household must be compared with its own specified threshold. Equal measured income need not imply equal classification.

before.q: Redistribution proposal L: Why might a libertarian object to redistribution even if it narrows measured inequality?
options: A lower Gini always reduces freedom
The policy may violate rights to legitimately acquired income or property
All transfers are in kind
Markets never generate income differences
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Redistribution Philosophy and Equity-Efficiency Tradeoffs.
before.feedback: Libertarian evaluation emphasizes the process by which holdings are acquired rather than equality of outcomes alone.

after.q: One policy restores property proven to have been stolen; another redistributes legitimately acquired property to equalize incomes. Both lower inequality. What follows under an entitlement framework?
options: Both must be rejected because an entitlement framework prohibits any change in ownership.
The first may rectify a rights violation; the common distributional result does not make the two policies equivalent.
Both must be accepted because lower inequality is the sole entitlement criterion.
Neither can be assessed without knowing whether aggregate income rises.
after.feedback: Rectification of unjust acquisition differs from compulsory equalization of legitimate holdings. A shared effect on inequality does not erase that distinction.

before.q: Antipoverty design G: How can a gradual benefit phaseout reduce a benefits cliff?
options: It spreads benefit reductions across a wider earnings range
It removes all work disincentives
It makes eligibility independent of income
It guarantees lower program cost
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Antipoverty Policy Design.
before.feedback: A gradual phaseout avoids one abrupt loss, although it can expose more recipients to a moderate effective marginal tax rate.

after.q: A program replaces a $1,000 benefit cliff at one earnings cutoff with a $0.20 reduction per dollar over the next $5,000. Which assessment is correct?
options: The abrupt $1,000 loss disappears, but the 20% phaseout weakens the marginal return to earnings across a wider range.
All work disincentives disappear because there is no longer a cliff.
The phaseout removes the benefit after only $200 of additional earnings.
Recipients throughout the phaseout keep every additional earnings dollar.
after.feedback: Spreading $1,000 over $5,000 produces a 20% phaseout. It smooths the discontinuity while applying a marginal benefit loss over the range.

before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Gini Coefficients.

before.q: Labor-market case J: Two otherwise similar jobs pay differently because one exposes workers to substantial danger. What can explain the pay gap?
options: A poverty threshold
A Lorenz-curve crossing
An in-kind transfer
A compensating wage differential
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Sources of Income Differences.
before.feedback: A riskier or less pleasant job may need to pay more to attract workers.

after.q: A dangerous job pays more than a safe job, but its workers also have more training. After training is controlled for, the wage gap shrinks but remains positive. What does this evidence support?
options: Training explains the entire gap; the remaining difference is evidence against risk compensation.
Risk compensation explains the entire gap; the training adjustment is irrelevant.
The remaining gap measures inherited wealth rather than labor income.
Training explains part of the gap; the remainder is consistent with risk compensation but is not uniquely identified as such.
after.feedback: The observed gap mixes worker characteristics and job attributes. Controlling for training removes one competing explanation but does not establish that no other differences remain.

before.q: Transfer-program case L: Why might a recipient prefer an equal-value cash transfer to a restricted food benefit?
options: Cash can be spent only on food
Cash permits spending on the recipient's highest-priority need
Cash always costs the government less
Restricted benefits never provide value
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by In-Kind Transfers.
before.feedback: Unrestricted cash expands choice, though policymakers may prefer targeting for paternalistic or political reasons.

after.q: An equal-cost cash grant gives recipients more choice than a restricted tutoring benefit. Suppose tutoring produces an external benefit not reflected in recipients’ choices. Which assessment is justified?
options: The external benefit makes the restricted benefit privately preferred by every recipient.
Cash weakly expands private choice; the external benefit gives a separate reason a policymaker might favor tutoring.
Greater private choice proves cash creates more total social benefit in every case.
Equal fiscal cost makes the restriction and the external benefit irrelevant.
after.feedback: Private choice and social spillovers are distinct criteria. An external benefit can motivate targeting even when recipients would choose another use for cash.

before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.
Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. What share goes to the bottom 60 percent?
options: 15 percent
40 percent
30 percent
70 percent
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.
before.feedback: The Lorenz point at cumulative population 60 is cumulative income 30.

after.q: Use the Lorenz curve. If total income is $200 million, how much goes to the bottom 60%, and why would assigning them $120 million misread the graph?
options: $120 million; the equality line gives the observed income distribution.
$140 million; subtract their 30% income share from 100%.
$60 million; 60% is their population share, while their income share is 30%.
$30 million; treat the percentage income share as a dollar amount.
after.feedback: The curve assigns 30% of income to the bottom 60% of people. 0.30×$200 million=$60 million; equal population shares do not imply equal income shares.

before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.
Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Why does the curve bow below the equality line?
options: Every household has identical income
Income is distributed unequally
The graph measures only poverty
Cumulative income can exceed 100 percent
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.
before.feedback: Lower-income cumulative groups receive less than their equal-population share.

after.q: The Lorenz curve gives the bottom 40% of households 15% of income. An analyst says this means their average income is 15% of the economy-wide mean. Which correction is right?
options: Their mean is 15% of the overall mean: use the cumulative income share alone.
Their mean is 37.5% of the overall mean: divide the income share by the population share.
Their mean is 40% of the overall mean: use the cumulative population share alone.
Their mean is 60% of the overall mean: use the population share outside this group.
after.feedback: The group receives 0.15 of income across 0.40 of households, so its average relative to the overall mean is 0.15/0.40=0.375.

before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Gini Coefficients.
Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Comparing Inequality.
