before.q: Refer to the graph above. How do bottom-40-percent income shares compare?
options: A gives 7 percent and B gives 22 percent
Both give 40 percent
A gives 78 percent and B gives 93 percent
A gives 22 percent and B gives 7 percent
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Comparing Inequality.
before.feedback: The highlighted readings at population 40 are 22 on A and 7 on B.

after.q: The graph assigns the bottom 40% a 22% income share in A and 7% in B. A has total income $100 million and B has $400 million. Which comparison distinguishes relative distribution from group income?
options: A has both the larger share and larger group income because 22% exceeds 7%.
B has the larger bottom-40% share because its total income is four times A’s.
The group receives equal income in A and B because each contains 40% of its population.
A has the larger bottom-40% share, but that group receives $22 million in A versus $28 million in B.
after.feedback: A’s group receives 0.22×100=$22 million; B’s receives 0.07×400=$28 million. Relative shares and absolute income totals answer different questions.

Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Comparing Inequality.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what is the top-quintile share under B?
options: About 40 percent
About 65 percent
About 60 percent
About 93 percent
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Comparing Inequality.
before.feedback: B gives the bottom 80 percent about 40 percent, leaving approximately 60 percent for the top quintile.

after.q: Under curve B, the bottom 80% receive approximately 40% of income. A student assigns the remaining 60% to the top 40% of households. What is the correct group and average-income comparison?
options: It is the top 40%; its mean income is about 1.5 times the overall mean.
It is the top 20%; its mean income is about 0.6 times the overall mean.
It is the top 20%; its mean income is about three times the overall mean.
It is the bottom 20%; its mean income is about three times the overall mean.
after.feedback: The complement of the bottom 80% is the top 20%. It receives 60% of income, so its mean relative to the overall mean is 0.60/0.20=3.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what share goes to households between the 40th and 60th percentiles under A?
options: About 22 percent
About 18 percent
About 40 percent
About 62 percent
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Lorenz Curves.
before.feedback: Subtract the graph readings: about 40 percent at the 60th percentile minus the labeled 22 percent at the 40th is about 18 percent.

after.q: Under curve A, cumulative income shares are approximately 22% at population 40% and 40% at population 60%. An analyst claims the intervening quintile has average income twice the economy-wide mean. Which correction fits the readings?
options: The quintile receives 40% of income, so its mean is twice the overall mean.
The quintile receives 18% of income, so its mean is about 90% of the overall mean.
The quintile receives 22% of income, so its mean is 110% of the overall mean.
The quintile receives 62% of income, so its mean is 310% of the overall mean.
after.feedback: The noncumulative share is 40−22=18%. Spread over 20% of households, this is 18/20=90% of the overall mean.

before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Gini Coefficients.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Could mean income fall even while the displayed Gini falls?
options: No, equality always raises mean income
No, Gini is average income
Only if the curve crosses equality
Yes; Gini measures relative distribution, not the income level
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Gini Coefficients.
before.feedback: Scale and distribution are separate; a lower relative-inequality measure does not determine the mean.

after.q: In the graph, the Gini falls and the Lorenz curve moves toward equality. Could a uniform 10% reduction in every household’s income, with nothing else changing, generate that distributional change?
options: Yes; a uniform proportional reduction necessarily moves the Lorenz curve toward equality.
Yes; a uniform proportional reduction eliminates the income gaps measured in percentages.
No; a uniform proportional reduction raises the Gini even though relative shares do not change.
No; a uniform proportional reduction lowers mean income but leaves relative income shares and the Gini unchanged.
after.feedback: Multiplying every income by 0.9 multiplies each group’s income and the total by the same factor. Shares and relative inequality do not change, so the displayed Gini decline requires a distributional change.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. Which fact alone proves the bottom and top quintiles receive different shares?
options: Both groups contain 20 percent of households
The bottom quintile receives 5 percent while the top quintile receives 45 percent
The curve begins at zero
The axes use percentages
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Comparing Inequality.
before.feedback: The cumulative readings yield a 5-percent bottom share and a 45-percent top share.

after.q: The graph initially gives the lowest quintile 5% of income and the highest quintile 45%. Total income is initially $100 million. Later total income rises to $120 million, the bottom share falls to 4% and the top share falls to 40%. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both groups lose income because both shares fall.
Bottom income falls from $5 million to $4.8 million; top income rises from $45 million to $48 million despite its smaller share.
Both groups gain income because total income rises.
Bottom income rises to $6 million and top income falls to $40 million because shares should be applied to the original total.
after.feedback: Compute each group’s share of the corresponding total. Bottom: 0.05×100=5 versus 0.04×120=4.8. Top: 0.45×100=45 versus 0.40×120=48. A changing share does not by itself establish the change in dollars.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. By how many points does the Gini fall?
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Gini Coefficients.
before.feedback: Subtract the after value 0.252 from the before value 0.380 to obtain a decline of 0.128.

after.q: The graph’s Gini falls from 0.380 to 0.252. Average real income also falls from $20,000 to $18,000. A report says the lower Gini proves higher living standards for every group. Which assessment is correct?
options: The Gini falls by 0.128, which proves every group’s real income rises despite the lower mean.
The Gini falls by 0.128 and average income by 10%; reduced relative inequality does not prove every group is better off.
The Gini rises by 0.128 because lower average income necessarily increases relative inequality.
The Gini falls by 12.8 income dollars per household, exactly offsetting the $2,000 income decline.
after.feedback: The Gini change is 0.380−0.252=0.128; mean income falls 2,000/20,000=10%. Distribution and income level must be assessed separately.

before.q: Refer to the graph above. At the 40-percent population mark, how large is the vertical gap from equality?
options: 15 percentage points
25 percentage points
40 percentage points
55 percentage points
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Gini Coefficients.
before.feedback: Perfect equality gives 40 percent while the Lorenz curve gives 15 percent, so the gap is 25 percentage points.

after.q: At the 40% population point, the graph gives cumulative income of 15%. A student reports a Gini of 0.25 by subtracting 0.15 from 0.40. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: The Gini is 0.25 because every pointwise vertical gap equals the entire inequality area.
The 25-percentage-point gap is valid at that point, but Gini depends on the area between the entire Lorenz curve and equality.
The correct Gini is 0.55 because cumulative income and population shares should be added.
The gap is 15 percentage points because the equality line is horizontal at 30%.
after.feedback: The pointwise gap is 40−15=25 percentage points. It is one height, not the area-based Gini; the rest of the distribution matters.

before.q: In hypothetical Economy D, the highest-income quintile receives 45% of income while the lowest-income quintile receives 5%. How many times as large is the highest quintile's share?
options: Five times as large
Nine times as large
Forty times as large
Fifty times as large
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Income Distribution and Measurement.
before.feedback: Divide 45 percent by 5 percent to compare the two noncumulative shares.

after.q: Initially the top quintile receives 45% of income and the bottom quintile 5%. A policy shifts five percentage points of total income from the top to the bottom, with total income and rankings unchanged. What happens to the top-to-bottom share ratio?
options: It falls from 9 to 8 because transferring five percentage points changes the ratio by one.
It falls from 9 to 4, but this change alone does not establish how much the entire distribution’s Gini changes.
It rises from 9 to 10 because the bottom share rises to 10%.
It stays at 9 because transfers cannot change relative income shares.
after.feedback: The original ratio is 45/5=9. New shares are 40% and 10%, giving 40/10=4. The full Lorenz distribution is needed for the Gini change.

before.q: In hypothetical Economy P, the highest-income quintile receives 45% of income while the lowest-income quintile receives 5%. How many times as large is the highest quintile's share?
options: Five times as large
Nine times as large
Forty times as large
Fifty times as large
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Income Distribution and Measurement.
before.feedback: Divide 45 percent by 5 percent to compare the two noncumulative shares.

after.q: The top quintile initially receives nine times the bottom quintile’s share: 45% versus 5%. A policy keeps their combined 50% share fixed but aims for a ratio of four. Which new shares meet both conditions?
options: Top 36%, bottom 9%; the ratio is four and their combined share remains 50%.
Top 40%, bottom 10%; shift five percentage points from top to bottom.
Top 45%, bottom 11.25%; preserve the top share and the original combined share.
Top 25%, bottom 25%; equal shares give a ratio of four.
after.feedback: Let the bottom share be b and the top 4b. Their sum is 5b=50%, so b=10% and top=40%. Both the target ratio and the combined-share constraint must hold.

before.q: For hypothetical Economy B, distribution A's Lorenz curve lies everywhere above B's and below equality. Which ordering follows?
options: A is more unequal than B
The distributions must have the same Gini
Only their mean incomes can be compared
A is less unequal than B
before.commonError: Uses a neighboring rule instead of the evidence required by Comparing Inequality.
before.feedback: A curve closer to equality Lorenz-dominates the lower curve and has a smaller inequality area.

after.q: Distribution A’s Lorenz curve lies everywhere above B’s and below equality. A has mean income $15,000 and B $25,000. Which judgment is supported without imposing an equity preference?
options: A has less relative inequality, so every household in A must have a higher real income than its counterpart in B.
B has less relative inequality because its mean income is higher.
The two distributions have identical inequality because both Lorenz curves end at 100%.
A has less relative inequality, but its lower mean prevents concluding from Lorenz dominance alone that its households have higher real incomes.
after.feedback: Lorenz dominance ranks relative inequality, not income levels. A’s higher curve and lower mean can coexist; the welfare comparison needs more information or explicit value judgments.

Treat the single report as more representative than the large dataset.

before.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

after.q: A crop price rises after a drought reduces harvests. A separate processing plant also discharges unpriced waste into a river. Which diagnosis and targeted response distinguish scarcity from market failure?
options: The crop price can signal genuine scarcity; a policy aimed at the waste should target its external cost rather than treating the high price alone as proof of failure.
Both are market failures solely because prices and waste increased, so a price ceiling necessarily corrects both.
Neither can be market failure because any outcome with a market price is efficient.
The drought is asymmetric information and the waste is merely a transfer between buyers and sellers.
after.feedback: A supply loss can raise a competitive price without creating a distortion. Unpriced harm omits social cost from the private decision and calls for a response to that specific wedge.

before.q: A seller hides product risk that buyers cannot observe. What mechanism applies?
options: Both sides possess the same relevant information
Asymmetric information
The problem is only that future outcomes are uncertain
A spillover harms an unrelated third party
before.feedback: Asymmetric information means one side holds relevant information the other lacks.

after.q: Buyers cannot observe product risk before purchase. Mandatory disclosure accurately reports it, but only in a format most buyers cannot interpret. A simplified tested label helps buyers compare risks at lower reading cost. Which comparison is defensible?
options: Accurate disclosure necessarily eliminates the problem regardless of comprehension, so testing the label adds no information.
Both address an information problem, but the tested label can improve usable information more effectively; accuracy alone does not establish that the first format changes decisions.
The unreadable format solves an externality while the label creates monopoly power.
Neither addresses market failure because information costs cannot affect mutually beneficial trades.
after.feedback: The original problem is an information gap about risk. Disclosure must be usable to affect choices; evidence about comprehension and behavior distinguishes formal disclosure from an effective remedy.

before.q: A corrective policy has large administrative costs. What must be compared?
options: Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
Administrative incentives and information do not matter
The remedy’s benefits and implementation costs
Any intervention is automatically costless
before.feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

after.q: A corrective policy would prevent $120 of external harm while using $35 of compliance resources and $100 of administrative resources. A simpler policy prevents $80 of harm and uses $20 in total resources. Which recommendation follows from these estimates alone?
options: The full policy is preferable because it prevents more harm, regardless of implementation cost.
Both policies are equally desirable because each reduces a market failure.
The full policy has net benefit −$15 and the simpler policy +$60; the simpler remedy is preferable to both the full policy and doing nothing.
Doing nothing is preferable because any administrative cost makes intervention inefficient.
after.feedback: Net benefits are 120−35−100=−15 and 80−20=60. The scale of the original failure does not make every proposed correction worthwhile.

before.q: A disclosure mandate improves information but confuses many buyers. What follows?
options: Any intervention is automatically costless
Identifying failure proves one remedy is optimal
A plausible remedy still requires evidence about real performance
Administrative incentives and information do not matter
before.feedback: Compare feasible responses, administrative costs, information limits, and unintended effects.

after.q: A disclosure rule is forecast to prevent $90 of harm at $20 resource cost. A pilot finds that confusion causes $35 of additional harm and that only $50 of the original harm is actually prevented. A simpler label prevents $40 at $10 cost with no added confusion. Which comparison uses the observed performance?
options: The original rule has +$70 net benefit because forecasts should replace contradictory pilot evidence.
The original rule has +$30 net benefit because confusion is only a transfer, making it equivalent to the simpler label.
The original rule has net benefit −$5, while the simpler label has +$30; revise the policy despite its initially plausible mechanism.
Neither can be compared because any information rule guarantees an efficient outcome.
after.feedback: Use the pilot’s actual effects: 50−35−20=−5. The alternative yields 40−10=30. The intended mechanism is relevant, but implementation evidence determines the net result.

before.q: An unequal outcome has no identified spillover, power, public-good, resource, or information problem. What can be concluded?
options: Inequality alone does not establish textbook market failure
A high price by itself establishes market failure
The outcome is disliked but no incentive wedge is identified
Inequality alone proves productive inefficiency
before.feedback: Market failure requires a specific reason private incentives diverge from efficient social outcomes.

after.q: A market maximizes measured total surplus but distributes it unequally; no externality, information gap, market power or public-good problem is identified. Policy A transfers $30 between participants without resource cost or changed behavior. Policy B makes the same transfer but destroys $8 of gains through changed allocation. Which assessment is correct?
options: Inequality motivates a separate equity judgment; A preserves measured surplus while B trades $8 of it for the same intended redistribution.
Both policies correct a demonstrated efficiency failure because any unequal outcome is inefficient.
B must be more efficient because changing allocation proves it addresses a market failure.
A raises total surplus by $30 while B raises it by $22 because transfers are new resources.
after.feedback: An unequal split does not by itself demonstrate a missing efficiency condition. The costless transfer changes distribution; B additionally sacrifices $8 of gains. Whether that tradeoff is acceptable requires an equity judgment.

after.q: Summit Coffee has demand P=118−2.2Q and MC=18+0.32Q. A new rival enters and lowers the demand intercept by $12. Demand slope and the entire cost function stay unchanged. Compared with the original profit-maximizing outcome, how do price and maximum economic profit change?
options: Price rises and profit falls: the lower quantity must raise the price along the original demand curve.
Price is unchanged and profit falls: unchanged MC fixes price at its original level.
Price falls and profit is unchanged: output adjustment fully offsets the demand reduction.
Both fall: weaker demand lowers the chosen price and the maximum profit obtainable from the unchanged cost curve.
after.feedback: The lower demand intercept reduces MR and the optimal output. With the stated linear demand and upward-sloping MC, price also falls. Revenue is lower at every positive output while costs are unchanged, so reoptimizing does not preserve the original maximum profit.

before.q: Which structure generally has more close substitutes for each firm’s product?
options: Monopolistic competition
Pure monopoly
Both have none
The answer depends only on fixed cost
before.feedback: Many differentiated rivals supply close alternatives.

after.q: A town has one water supplier with no close substitute and many restaurants offering differentiated meals. For which seller is switching to a close rival’s product generally easier?
options: A restaurant
The water supplier
Both have no substitutes
Neither, because differentiation prevents substitution
after.feedback: Restaurant alternatives are close substitutes despite differentiation; the water supplier is specified to lack a close substitute.

before.q: Which model can sustain long-run economic profit because barriers block entry?
options: Monopolistic competition
Monopoly
Both by definition
Neither
before.feedback: Entry erodes profit in monopolistic competition.

after.q: Firm A’s profit attracts unrestricted entry; firm B’s profit is protected by an effective entry barrier. Which can more readily sustain positive economic profit in the long run?
options: A
B
Both must lose all profit immediately
Neither can ever earn economic profit
after.feedback: The barrier prevents the entry response that would otherwise erode B’s profit.

before.q: More close substitutes make a firm’s demand:
options: Less elastic
Perfectly inelastic
More elastic
Unrelated to price
before.feedback: Substitution opportunities increase responsiveness.

after.q: Before close substitutes enter, a 5% price increase reduces a firm’s quantity by 2%. After entry, the same price increase reduces quantity by 8%. What happens to demand elasticity magnitude?
options: It falls from 1.6 to 0.4.
It stays at 5.
It rises from 0.4 to 1.6.
It rises from 2.5 to 4.
after.feedback: Use |%ΔQ/%ΔP|: 2/5=0.4 and 8/5=1.6. More substitutes are consistent with greater responsiveness.

before.q: Cost analysis tells a differentiated firm its MC curve. Which additional curve is needed to apply the usual profit-maximizing output rule?
options: Market supply
Marginal revenue
Average fixed cost
Long-run average cost
before.commonError: misapplies_monopolistic_competition_rule
before.feedback: A monopolistically competitive firm chooses output where MR equals MC, subject to the usual marginal condition.

after.q: A firm has MR=40−2Q and constant MC=12. At what output do these curves meet?
after.feedback: 40−2Q=12 gives 2Q=28 and Q=14.

before.q: The shutdown rule from cost analysis carries directly into monopolistic competition. Which comparison determines whether the firm should produce in the short run?
options: Price compared with AVC at the chosen output
Price compared with AFC at the chosen output
Marginal revenue compared with ATC
Total revenue compared only with fixed cost
before.commonError: misapplies_monopolistic_competition_rule
before.feedback: A firm should produce in the short run when price covers average variable cost at its profit-maximizing output.

after.q: At its best positive output a firm receives P=$20 and has AVC=$16, ATC=$23. Fixed costs are unavoidable now. What should it do this period?
options: Operate despite an economic loss.
Shut down because P is below ATC.
Operate because it earns positive economic profit.
Shut down because P exceeds AVC.
after.feedback: Each unit contributes $4 toward unavoidable fixed cost, so operation is better than shutdown despite the $3 per-unit total-cost loss.

before.q: A firm has already selected output where MR=MC. Which comparison now determines whether it earns profit or loss?
options: Price compared with MC
MR compared with AVC
Demand compared with market supply
Price compared with ATC
before.commonError: misapplies_monopolistic_competition_rule
before.feedback: At the chosen output, price above ATC means profit, price below ATC means loss, and equality means zero economic profit.

after.q: A differentiated firm chooses 50 units with P=$18 and ATC=$20. What is economic profit?

before.q: Elasticity analysis helps explain branding. If brand loyalty reduces the absolute value of price elasticity of demand, buyers become:
options: Completely unwilling to buy
Perfectly responsive at one market price
Less responsive to the firm’s price
More responsive to the firm’s price
before.commonError: misapplies_monopolistic_competition_rule
before.feedback: Lower absolute elasticity means quantity demanded changes less for a given percentage price change.

after.q: After a branding campaign, the magnitude of price elasticity falls from 2 to 0.5. Using the small-change approximation, what quantity response follows a 4% price increase after the campaign?
options: An 8% decrease
A 2% increase
A 2% decrease
A 0.5% decrease
after.feedback: The postcampaign response is −0.5×4%=−2%.

before.q: A successful new product feature creates short-run profit in a market with easy entry. What long-run force can erode that profit?
options: Entry and imitation by rivals
A permanent legal ban on substitutes
Automatic shutdown of the innovating firm
A requirement that demand become perfectly inelastic
before.commonError: misapplies_monopolistic_competition_rule
before.feedback: With relatively easy entry and close substitutes, successful differentiation can attract rivals and imitation over time.

after.q: A new product feature earns short-run profit, but rivals can copy it and enter freely. What response would tend to erode the innovator’s profit?
options: Rivals introduce close alternatives that draw away some of its demand.
Rivals’ entry guarantees the innovator a permanent monopoly.
Imitation raises every buyer’s reservation value for the original by definition.
Entry eliminates the innovator’s fixed costs.
after.feedback: Imitation and entry expand the alternatives available to buyers, weakening the original firm’s demand advantage.

before.q: For Apex Water Authority, the competitive benchmark output is 38.18 rather than monopoly output 20. Which welfare statement is correct?
options: Output between Qm and Qc has value above MC
Output below Qm has price below marginal cost
Output beyond Qc has value above marginal cost
The output gap consists solely of monopoly profit
before.feedback: The monopoly restriction leaves positive-surplus units unproduced.

after.q: Apex Water Authority has demand P=100−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. A regulator proposes marginal-cost pricing with a lump-sum subsidy to cover the fixed cost. Raising subsidy funds creates no additional distortion, but administration uses $50 of real resources. Compared with the unregulated monopoly, which welfare accounting is correct?
options: Output rises from 20 to 40; eliminating DWL adds $400, and net surplus rises $350 after administration.
Output rises from 20 to 40; subtract the $200 subsidy itself as a further resource loss, giving $150.
Output stays at 20; the subsidy covers fixed cost but cannot change a regulated output.
Output rises from 20 to 40; the entire $400 gain is a transfer to consumers, so net surplus falls $50.
after.feedback: MR=100−4Q gives Qm=20 and Pm=60. Demand=MC gives Qc=40; the recovered triangular gains are 0.5×20×40=$400. The subsidy is a transfer under the stated financing assumption; administration is a real incremental cost.

after.q: Beacon Patent Systems has demand P=104−2Q, constant MC=$20, and an unavoidable fixed production cost of $200 over the comparison period. Monopoly price rises from $82 to $77, and the efficient-output benchmark stays at 62.

after.feedback: After innovation Qm=(144−10)/4=33.5, Pm=77, and Qc=67. The new triangle is 0.5×33.5×67=$1122.25, versus $961 originally. A lower monopoly price can coexist with a larger gap from the new efficient benchmark.

before.q: Which cost curve determines the monopolist’s output at the margin?
options: Average fixed cost
Average total cost alone
Total fixed cost
Marginal cost
before.feedback: MR is compared with MC for output choice.

after.q: A monopolist has MR=50−2Q and MC=10. What output solves MR=MC?
after.feedback: 50−2Q=10 implies Q=20.

before.q: Which cost measure determines monopoly profit per unit after output and price are chosen?
options: Average total cost
Marginal cost
Average fixed cost only
Total variable cost
before.feedback: Profit per unit is P−ATC.

after.q: After choosing output, a monopolist charges $40 and has ATC=$28. What is economic profit per unit?
after.feedback: Price minus ATC is 40−28=$12 per unit.

before.q: Which cost threshold governs short-run monopoly shutdown?
options: Minimum ATC
Minimum AFC
Minimum AVC
Maximum MC
before.feedback: The firm must cover avoidable variable cost.

after.q: At its best positive output a monopolist has total revenue $500 and variable cost $540. Fixed cost of $100 is unavoidable now. What should it do this period?
options: Operate because revenue is positive.
Operate because revenue exceeds fixed cost.
Shut down, avoiding the $40 shortfall on variable cost.
Shut down to avoid the fixed cost as well.
after.feedback: Operation loses $140; shutdown loses the unavoidable $100 only. The $40 variable-cost shortfall makes shutdown better.

before.q: At the quantity where total revenue is maximized, demand is unit elastic and MR is:
options: Equal to price
Zero
Equal to ATC
At its maximum
before.feedback: The derivative or marginal change in TR is zero at the maximum.

after.q: For demand P=20−Q, total revenue is maximized at Q=10. MR=20−2Q. What is MR at that output?
after.feedback: MR at Q=10 is 20−20=0, matching the total-revenue maximum.

before.q: Why does reducing monopoly output below the competitive quantity create DWL?
options: All producer surplus disappears
ATC necessarily rises
Demand becomes perfectly elastic
Some buyers value omitted units above their marginal cost
before.feedback: The omitted units would generate positive gains from trade.

after.q: A monopolist omits a unit worth $18 to a buyer that would cost $12 to produce. With no external effects, how much surplus is lost on that omitted unit?
after.feedback: The forgone gain from trade is value minus marginal cost: 18−12=$6.

before.q: What marginal comparison determines monopoly output?
options: Price compared with ATC
MR compared with MC
TR compared with fixed cost only
Demand compared with AVC
before.feedback: Produce units whose marginal revenue covers marginal cost.

after.q: The next unit would add $14 to a monopolist’s revenue and $18 to its cost. Should the firm add it?
options: Yes; it would increase profit by $4.
No; it would reduce profit by $4.
Yes; all additional sales increase profit.
No; the lost profit equals the full $18 cost.

before.q: How do barriers to entry connect monopoly structure to persistent economic profit?
options: They make total cost independent of output
They guarantee that the monopolist chooses the efficient quantity
They prevent new rivals from entering quickly when profit appears
They force demand to become perfectly elastic
before.feedback: Barriers can keep profit from triggering the entry response that erodes profit in competitive markets.

after.q: A profitable incumbent has an exclusive legal right to supply a product, and potential rivals cannot enter during its term. What mechanism can preserve its profit?

The exclusive right makes every buyer’s demand perfectly elastic.
The barrier blocks the entry response to profit.
Potential entry necessarily expands supply during the prohibition.
after.feedback: When entry is blocked, profit need not attract the new supply that would otherwise erode it.

before.q: What does positive marginal revenue tell you about the portion of a monopolist’s demand curve?

Demand must have unit elasticity at every output
Demand is elastic at that output
Demand is inelastic at that output
before.feedback: For a downward-sloping demand curve, MR is positive on the elastic portion.

after.q: At a point on smooth downward-sloping demand, P=$30 and |Ed|=3. Using MR=P(1−1/|Ed|), what is MR?
after.feedback: MR=30(1−1/3)=20, positive on this elastic segment.

before.q: How do monopoly revenue analysis and marginal cost combine into the output decision?
options: ATC determines quantity before revenue is considered
Price is chosen first and forces MR to equal MC
Demand generates MR, and the firm compares that MR with MC to choose quantity
Demand sets MC directly, so MR is unnecessary
before.feedback: The monopolist’s demand conditions determine MR; costs determine MC; their marginal comparison selects output.

after.q: A monopolist’s demand is P=30−Q, so MR=30−2Q; MC=10. What output satisfies its marginal rule?
after.feedback: Equate MR and MC: 30−2Q=10, so Q=10. Demand equal to MC would give a different, efficient benchmark.

before.q: Why is monopoly price determined only after the profit-maximizing quantity is chosen?
options: Average total cost sets price before marginal analysis begins
The firm first uses MR and MC to choose output, then demand reveals the highest single price consistent with that output
Price is unrelated to demand until output is produced
The monopolist has no control over quantity
before.feedback: Monopoly analysis is a two-step decision: marginal output choice first, demand-based price second.

after.q: A monopolist has already chosen Q=12 using MR=MC. Demand is P=50−2Q. What price supports that quantity?
after.feedback: Read price from demand at the selected output: 50−2(12)=$26.

before.q: Why might a subsidy accompany marginal-cost pricing for a natural monopoly?
options: The subsidy makes demand horizontal
A subsidy prevents all entry barriers
P=MC can leave revenue below total cost when ATC exceeds MC
A subsidy is required because MR always exceeds price
before.feedback: The subsidy addresses the financing gap created by efficient pricing when scale economies keep ATC above MC.

after.q: Under marginal-cost pricing a natural monopoly supplies 100 units at P=$8, while ATC=$11 at that output. What subsidy covers the total-cost shortfall?
after.feedback: The shortfall is (ATC−P)Q=(11−8)×100=$300.

before.q: How does elasticity connect directly to third-degree discriminatory pricing?
options: Elasticity determines fixed cost rather than price
Elasticity matters only under perfect competition
Groups with less elastic demand can sustain larger markups over marginal cost
More elastic groups always pay more
before.feedback: Different demand responsiveness is the economic reason separated groups can receive different optimal prices.

after.q: A firm can separate two customer groups without resale and faces the same positive constant MC for both. At their interior optima demand elasticities have magnitudes 2 and 4. Which group has the higher price under third-degree discrimination?
options: The group with elasticity magnitude 4
Both must have the same price
The group with elasticity magnitude 2
The group with more customers regardless of elasticity
after.feedback: MR=MC implies a larger markup for the less elastic group; with common MC, the |Ed|=2 group has the higher price.

after.q: Two rival cruise lines keep fares at $72 and sell 30 units each in the kinked-demand model shown. Rivals match fare cuts but do not match fare increases. A per-unit cost increase raises this firm’s constant MC from $48 to $54, with demand and fixed cost unchanged. How do its profit-maximizing fare, quantity and economic profit change?
options: Fare rises to $78 and quantity stays at 30; economic profit is unchanged.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit is unchanged because MR has a gap.
Fare falls and quantity rises; economic profit falls by less than $180.
Fare and quantity stay at $72 and 30; economic profit falls by $180.
after.feedback: At Q=30 the MR gap runs from $36 to $60. Both MC=$48 and MC=$54 fall inside it, so the optimum remains at the kink, P=$72 and Q=30. Cost rises $6 on each of 30 units, lowering profit by $180.
after.imageAlt: Kinked demand at quantity 30, price 72, with two MR branches and MC at 48.
after.graphDescription: Quantity is horizontal and dollars per unit vertical. Demand follows P=84−0.4Q for Q up to 30, then P=108−1.2Q for larger Q. At Q=30, the upper MR branch ends at 60 and the lower branch begins at 36. MC is horizontal at 48.

after.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown: P=70−0.5Q up to Q=20 and P=90−1.5Q above Q=20. Its constant MC initially equals $40. Compare a rise in MC to $45 with a rise to $55, holding demand fixed. Which conclusion is correct?
options: At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50.
At MC=$45 and MC=$55 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60 because any cost change lies inside the MR gap.
At MC=$45 the firm keeps Q=20 and P=$60; at MC=$55 it expands output to Q=25 and lowers price to $52.50.
At MC=$45 it reduces output to Q=15 and raises price to $62.50; at MC=$55 it returns to Q=20 and P=$60.
after.feedback: At the kink MR drops from $50 to $30. MC=$45 lies within that range, but MC=$55 lies above it. On the upper demand branch MR=70−Q, so 70−Q=55 gives Q=15 and P=70−0.5×15=$62.50.

after.q: A firm faces the kinked demand shown, with prevailing price $72, quantity 30 and constant MC=$48. An input improvement lowers MC to $42, while a recurring license fee adds $300 to fixed cost. Demand does not change. Which evaluation correctly separates the output decision from the profit effect?
options: Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving exceeds the $300 fee, so economic profit rises by $120.
Price and quantity stay at the kink; the $180 variable-cost saving is smaller than the $300 fee, so economic profit falls by $120.
The fixed fee raises MC above the MR gap, so quantity falls; the variable-cost saving cannot affect profit.
The lower MC moves quantity above the kink; the fixed fee is a variable cost, so profit is unchanged.
after.feedback: The MR gap at Q=30 is $36 to $60; MC=$42 remains inside it, so P and Q stay at $72 and 30. Variable cost falls by ($48−$42)×30=$180. The $300 fixed fee does not enter MC but exceeds that saving, reducing profit by $120.

before.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. Which outcome maximizes the firms’ combined payoff?
options: Row B, Column Y
Row A, Column Y
Row A, Column X
Row B, Column X
before.feedback: Solve best responses and compare them with combined payoffs.

after.q: Use the displayed payoff matrix as the baseline. An enforceable agreement deducts 3 from the row firm’s payoff whenever it chooses B and 3 from the column firm’s payoff whenever it chooses Y, in every cell. Which comparison with the original game is correct?
options: The unique Nash outcome remains (B,Y) because an output-independent agreement cannot change any payoff.
Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are Nash outcomes after the deductions because the penalty leaves best responses unchanged.
The unique Nash outcome changes from (B,Y) to (A,X); (A,X) also remains the joint-payoff maximum.
The unique Nash outcome becomes (A,Y), because only the row firm changes its response.
after.feedback: Originally each firm prefers its noncooperative action. After deductions, row payoffs are A/X=10, A/Y=6, B/X=9, B/Y=5, so A is best against either column. Column payoffs analogously make X best against either row. Thus (A,X) is the unique equilibrium and gives the highest combined payoff, 20.

before.q: Refer to the payoff matrix. Which strategies form the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: Row B, Column Y
Row A, Column X
Row A, Column Y
Row B, Column X
before.feedback: Solve best responses and compare them with combined payoffs.

after.q: Use the displayed payoff matrix as the baseline. A coordination program adds 6 to each firm’s payoff only at (A,X), leaving all other cells unchanged. Which list contains all pure-strategy Nash equilibria after the change, and which outcome maximizes joint payoff?
options: Both (A,X) and (B,Y) are equilibria; (A,X) maximizes joint payoff at 32.
Only (A,X) is an equilibrium; improving that cell removes the incentive to choose B against Y.
Only (B,Y) is an equilibrium; the added payoff cannot alter any best response.
Both (A,Y) and (B,X) are equilibria; their unequal payoffs maximize the joint total.
after.feedback: The new (A,X) payoff is (16,16), so A is preferred to B against X and X to Y against A. Against Y, row still prefers B (7>5), and against B, column still prefers Y (7>5). Thus the old (B,Y) equilibrium also remains, while (A,X) yields the highest joint payoff.

after.q: Market shares are 46%, 22%, 14%, 10% and 8%. The two smallest firms merge, with no other share changes. Which calculation and interpretation is correct?
options: CR4 stays 92% and HHI rises to 3120 because combining two small firms cannot change the top four.
CR4 rises to 100% and HHI stays 2960 because the combined market share is unchanged.
CR4 rises by 18 percentage points and HHI rises by 18 because the merging shares should be added to both indexes.
CR4 rises from 92% to 100% and HHI rises from 2960 to 3120; the measures describe concentration, not a complete prediction of conduct.
after.feedback: After merger the four shares are 46,22,18,14, so CR4=100%. The HHI increment is 2×10×8=160, making 3120. Conduct also depends on entry, substitution and behavior.

after.q: Market shares are 33%, 29%, 17%, 12% and 9%. Compare merger A (33% with 9%) with merger B (17% with 12%), holding other shares fixed. Which comparison is correct?
options: Both give CR4=100%, but A raises HHI by 594 and B by 408; equal CR4 does not imply the same HHI change.
Both give CR4=100% and the same HHI increase because each merger removes one firm.
A raises HHI less than B because one of its partners is the smallest firm.
CR4 stays 91% under both mergers because the original four largest shares are unchanged.
after.feedback: Each leaves four firms, so CR4 becomes 100%. HHI increments are 2×33×9=594 and 2×17×12=408. The product of the merging shares matters, not merely the smaller partner’s rank.

after.q: Market shares are 40%, 26%, 15%, 11% and 8%. The 40% firm is split into two independent competitors, each with 20%, and all other shares stay fixed. Which comparison with the original concentration measures is correct?
options: CR4 remains 92% and HHI remains 2686 because the two new firms have the same combined share.
CR4 falls from 92% to 81%, and HHI falls from 2686 to 1886; the new shares must be reranked.
CR4 falls to 72% and HHI falls by only 20 because one new share should be omitted.
CR4 rises to 100% and HHI rises to 3486 because there are more competitors.
after.feedback: The new top four shares are 26,20,20,15, totaling 81. Replace 40² by 20²+20², reducing HHI by 800 to 1886. Independence, not merely a new label, is required for this calculation.

after.feedback: The current largest maximizing output is 4, giving contribution $58 and profit $0. At the future price 7, even the first unit’s MC=8 exceeds price and later marginal costs are higher, so no positive output improves profit.

before.q: A competitive firm faces P = $34, TFC = $380, and marginal costs for units 1–7 of $9, $14, $20, $27, $35, $44, $54. Which output-profit pair is consistent with both marginal analysis and the firm’s total profit?
options: Q=4; economic loss of $314
Q=3; economic loss of $321
Q=5; economic loss of $315
Q=4; total revenue=$136
before.feedback: Use the marginal rule, then calculate total revenue minus total cost.

after.q: A competitive firm faces price $34. Fixed cost is $86, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [9, 14, 20, 27, 35, 44, 54] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. An accountant recommends immediate shutdown because profit is negative. Another adviser recommends operating now but exiting before the fixed cost can recur. Which comparison supports the better proposal?
options: Operating at 4 loses $20, less than the shutdown loss $86; exit later avoids the recurring loss if conditions persist.
Immediate shutdown loses $0, while operating loses $20; exit timing makes no difference.
Operating at 4 earns $66 of economic profit, so remain indefinitely.
Producing 7 units eliminates the fixed-cost loss because revenue rises with output.
after.feedback: At Q=4, contribution is $66, so the loss is $86−$66=$20. Shutdown still loses all $86 now. Next period the cost is avoidable through exit, changing the relevant alternative.

before.q: A competitive firm faces P = $37, TFC = $420, and marginal costs for units 1–7 of $10, $15, $21, $28, $36, $45, $55. Which output-profit pair is consistent with both marginal analysis and the firm’s total profit?
options: Q=4; economic loss of $346
Q=5; economic loss of $345
Q=6; economic loss of $353
Q=5; total revenue=$185
before.feedback: Use the marginal rule, then calculate total revenue minus total cost.

after.q: A competitive firm faces price $9. Fixed cost is $30, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. A verified process improvement lowers every marginal unit cost by $2, with fixed cost and price unchanged. Which counterfactual is correct?
options: Output stays at 0; only fixed-cost changes can affect an operating decision.
Output changes from 0 to 1; profit changes from $-30 to $-29, so the technology can change operation even if profit remains negative.
Output changes to 7 and profit becomes positive because every cost-saving innovation guarantees profit.
Output changes to 1; profit is $1 because the improvement eliminates the original fixed cost.
after.feedback: After the improvement, contributions at outputs 0–7 are [0, 1, -3, -13, -30, -55, -89, -133]. The largest maximum is Q=1 with contribution $1. Subtract unchanged F=$30 for profit $-29, compared with the original $-30.

before.q: A competitive firm faces P = $40, TFC = $460, and marginal costs for units 1–7 of $11, $16, $22, $29, $37, $46, $56. Which output-profit pair is consistent with both marginal analysis and the firm’s total profit?
options: Q=4; economic loss of $378
Q=6; economic loss of $381
Q=5; economic loss of $375
Q=5; total revenue=$200
before.feedback: Use the marginal rule, then calculate total revenue minus total cost.

after.q: A competitive firm faces price $40. Fixed cost is $115, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [11, 16, 22, 29, 37, 46, 56] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. A new unconditional license fee adds $15 to this period’s fixed cost. A manager proposes reducing output because the fee “raises MC.” Which correction is right?
options: Output falls to 4; profit rises because spreading fewer units over the fee lowers MC.
Output rises to 7; this necessarily recovers the fixed fee regardless of marginal cost.
Output remains 5; profit changes from $-30 to $-45, because the fee changes fixed cost but not the output contribution schedule.
Output remains 5; profit stays $-30 because fixed costs affect neither output nor profit.
after.feedback: Before the fee the best contribution is $85 at Q=5. Every output’s profit is reduced by the same $15, so the maximizing quantity is unchanged and profit becomes $-45.

before.q: A competitive firm faces P = $43, TFC = $500, and marginal costs for units 1–7 of $12, $17, $23, $30, $38, $47, $57. Which output-profit pair is consistent with both marginal analysis and the firm’s total profit?
options: Q=4; economic loss of $410
Q=6; economic loss of $409
Q=5; total revenue=$215
Q=5; economic loss of $405
before.feedback: Use the marginal rule, then calculate total revenue minus total cost.

after.q: A competitive firm faces price $43. Fixed cost is $85, unavoidable this period but avoidable by exiting before next period. Marginal costs of units 1–7 are [12, 17, 23, 30, 38, 47, 57] dollars; variable cost at zero output is zero. Choose the largest output if two quantities tie for maximum profit. Next period the price is expected to be $11, with marginal costs unchanged. Which comparison separates current operation from the response to that price?
options: Currently Q=5 and profit is $10; at $11, keep output 5 to spread fixed cost.
Currently Q=7 and profit is maximized; at $11, add units because their sales cover some fixed cost.
Currently Q=0 because fixed cost is positive; at $11, enter because a lower price means lower cost.
Currently Q=5 and profit is $10; at $11, every marginal unit costs more than its price, so choose zero output.
after.feedback: The current largest maximizing output is 5, giving contribution $95 and profit $10. At the future price 11, even the first unit’s MC=12 exceeds price and later marginal costs are higher, so no positive output improves profit.

before.q: Refer to the graph. The market panel sets P1. On the firm panel, which analytical order is valid?
options: Use market output as firm output; compare P1 with AVC and ATC
Choose minimum ATC output first; set MR equal to ATC rather than P1
Set MR = P1; find rising MC = MR; compare price with AVC and ATC
Choose firm price above P1 first; find output from the market demand curve
before.feedback: Link market price, firm output, operating status, and adjustment without confusing market and firm quantities.

after.q: Use the market and representative-firm panels. An analyst assigns the market’s total quantity to each firm and recommends producing at minimum ATC whenever that differs from the MR=MC quantity. Which correction preserves both the market-firm distinction and the operating decision?
options: Divide market price by the number of firms, assign market quantity to each firm, and use ATC alone to decide shutdown.
Take price from the market, but choose minimum ATC before considering MR; firms can then sell any desired amount at that cost.
Take price from the market, choose each operating firm’s output on rising MC at that price, and check AVC before production and ATC for profit.
Take the firm’s MC as the market demand curve, choose market quantity there, and ignore AVC if revenue is positive.
after.feedback: Market quantity is the sum of firms’ outputs, not the output of each firm. A price taker has MR=P; the candidate output satisfies rising MC=P when operating. AVC governs shutdown, while ATC determines economic profit.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Suppose the market price rises. What must happen before any long-run entry response?
options: Incumbents keep output fixed until new firms have entered
Incumbents choose output at minimum ATC regardless of price
Incumbents raise their own price without changing output
Incumbents compare the new price with MC, AVC, and ATC
before.feedback: Link market price, firm output, operating status, and adjustment without confusing market and firm quantities.

after.q: Use the two-panel graph. A permanent demand increase raises market price before entry can occur. Assume a constant-cost industry with free entry. Which sequence correctly separates an incumbent’s immediate response from the final industry outcome?
options: Incumbents keep output fixed until entry occurs; the additional firms permanently maintain the initial price increase.
Incumbents expand by shifting their MC curves right solely because market price rises; entry then raises price further.
Incumbents choose a higher individual selling price than the market; entry later forces every firm to minimum AVC.
Incumbents expand along rising MC and may earn profit; entry then expands market supply until price returns to the original long-run level.
after.feedback: The initial higher market price raises each price taker’s MR, changing its output on the existing MC curve. Profit induces entry. With industry expansion leaving firm costs unchanged, long-run price returns to the original zero-profit level.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Price lies above ATC at Q1. Which combined result follows?
options: Positive profit now; entry pressure if it persists
Shutdown now; exit pressure
Zero profit now
Loss now; entry pressure
before.feedback: Link market price, firm output, operating status, and adjustment without confusing market and firm quantities.

after.q: The graph initially shows P above ATC at Q1. An unavoidable fee for the current year raises fixed cost by more than the initial total profit, leaving demand, MC and AVC unchanged. The fee is avoidable by leaving before next year. Which sequence is correct?
options: Keep the same short-run output but incur a loss; if these conditions persist, exit can avoid the future fee.
Reduce short-run output because the fee raises MC; continue permanently because P still covers AVC.
Keep the same short-run output and profit because a fixed fee never affects profit.
Shut down immediately and avoid this year’s fee; reenter next year if P remains above AVC.
after.feedback: The fee does not change the MR=MC output or the current operating margin over variable cost. It does reduce profit, possibly below zero. A fee unavoidable now but avoidable next year separates short-run operation from long-run exit.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Price lies between AVC and ATC. Which combined result follows?
options: Shut down with zero loss
Operate with a loss now; exit pressure if it persists
Earn profit; entry pressure
Set a higher price
before.feedback: Link market price, firm output, operating status, and adjustment without confusing market and firm quantities.

after.q: The graph shows AVC<P<ATC at the operating quantity Q1. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. A student says shutting down removes the entire loss (ATC−P)Q1. Which comparison correctly evaluates production versus shutdown?
options: Producing incurs (ATC−P)Q1, while shutdown loses zero because all costs become avoidable immediately.
Producing incurs (ATC−P)Q1, while shutdown loses all fixed cost; producing covers (P−AVC)Q1 of that fixed cost and is preferable now.
Producing covers no fixed cost because P<ATC, so shutdown and production necessarily have identical losses.
Producing earns positive economic profit because P>AVC, so the stated loss rectangle should be ignored.
after.feedback: Revenue exceeds variable cost, so production contributes a positive amount toward unavoidable fixed cost. The operating loss is smaller than the fixed-cost loss under shutdown, although persistent losses can still lead to long-run exit.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Price lies below AVC. Which combined result follows?
options: Produce now; persistent losses necessarily attract entry
Shut down now; fixed costs are thereby eliminated
Shut down now; persistent losses can lead to exit
Produce at minimum ATC; all fixed costs are covered
before.feedback: Link market price, firm output, operating status, and adjustment without confusing market and firm quantities.

after.q: The graph shows a firm below its AVC shutdown threshold. Compare an unconditional lump-sum grant with a per-unit subsidy large enough to raise the firm’s net receipt above that threshold. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. Which operating comparison is correct?
options: Both policies change marginal receipts equally, so either grant necessarily restores production.
The lump-sum grant lowers MC and restores production, while the per-unit subsidy affects fixed cost only.
The lump-sum grant alone leaves the shutdown decision unchanged; the per-unit subsidy changes marginal receipts and can make production worthwhile.
Neither policy can change production because any firm with an initial loss must shut down forever.
after.feedback: An unconditional grant does not change the payoff difference between producing and not producing. A per-unit subsidy is earned only on output and changes the net price compared with MC and AVC, potentially crossing the operating threshold.

before.q: Refer to the graph. Which part of the cost structure maps into the firm’s short-run supply response?
options: ATC below AFC
Horizontal MR alone
All MC including below AVC
Rising MC above the AVC shutdown point
before.feedback: Link market price, firm output, operating status, and adjustment without confusing market and firm quantities.

after.q: Use the short-run supply graph. Compare a rise in unavoidable fixed rent with a rise in the variable cost of every unit produced, holding market demand unchanged. Which statement separates the two effects on firm supply?
options: Both costs shift short-run supply upward by the same amount because both increase ATC.
The fixed rent shifts short-run supply upward, while higher variable cost affects only long-run exit.
Neither cost affects supply until entry occurs because a price-taking firm cannot change output.
The fixed rent alone leaves MC and AVC, and thus short-run supply, unchanged; higher variable cost can raise MC and the shutdown threshold.
after.feedback: The operating supply relation uses rising MC above minimum AVC. Fixed rent does not enter either marginal or variable cost, although it affects profit and later exit. Variable-cost changes directly affect the operating comparison.

before.q: An external cost is discovered. Which combined firm-and-market conclusion is defensible?
options: Perfect competition automatically internalizes it
ATC becomes irrelevant
Zero profit guarantees social efficiency
Private P=MC may no longer identify the socially efficient output
before.feedback: Classify the cost or market failure and trace the short-run and long-run implications.

after.q: At the current competitive output, price equals private MC=$18. Each extra unit also imposes $6 of uncompensated harm on others. A proposal uses a $6 per-unit tax instead of an output-independent license payment of equal expected revenue. Which comparison targets the external-cost distortion?
options: Both payments make MC=$24 because equal government revenue implies equal marginal incentives.
The lump-sum payment corrects the distortion, while a per-unit tax affects only the distribution of profit.
Neither payment can affect efficiency because P=private MC already guarantees a social optimum.
The per-unit tax makes the firm face the $24 social marginal cost at that output; the lump-sum payment does not change its marginal production incentive.
after.feedback: Social MC adds the $6 external harm to private MC. A per-unit tax places that harm in the private marginal decision; an output-independent payment changes profit without adding the same marginal incentive.

before.q: P=MC and P=min ATC. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: Allocatively and productively efficient; zero economic profit
Allocatively efficient only; positive economic profit
Productively efficient only; zero economic profit
Neither form of efficiency; negative economic profit
before.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

after.q: A price-taking firm initially produces at the minimum of ATC, where P=MC=ATC=$18, with no externalities. A temporary mandate forces it farther along rising MC to an output where ATC=$20 and MC=$23; market price stays $18. Which comparison is correct?
options: The original output is productively and allocatively efficient with zero economic profit; the mandated output is neither and creates an economic loss.
Both outputs are productively efficient because the original minimum ATC remains $18; the mandated output earns zero profit.
The mandated output is allocatively efficient because more output is produced, although ATC exceeds price.
The original output is inefficient because profit is zero; the mandated output improves efficiency by raising ATC.
after.feedback: Initially the chosen output actually attains minimum ATC and P=MC. Under the mandate, ATC is above its minimum and MC exceeds marginal value P; P<ATC also means a loss. A minimum somewhere on the curve is not enough to establish efficiency at another output.

before.q: P>MC and P=min ATC. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The firm is allocatively efficient because producing at minimum ATC also implies that P=MC at this output
The firm should shut down because P>MC means the chosen output fails the short-run operating test
The firm is productively efficient at its output, but the price-output outcome is not allocatively efficient
The firm earns zero accounting profit because price equals minimum ATC at the chosen output
before.feedback: Apply the exact efficiency conditions and distinguish behavioral assumptions from welfare assumptions.

after.q: A price-taking firm faces a temporary output cap of 40 units. At 40 units, ATC is at its minimum of $12 and MC is $12; market price is $18. There are no externalities. If the cap is removed, rising MC reaches $18 at 70 units, where ATC exceeds its minimum. Which comparison correctly evaluates the two outputs?
options: At 40 units production is both productively and allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is neither.
At 40 units production is neither productively nor allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is both.
At 40 units production is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient; at 70 units it is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient.
At 40 units production is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient; at 70 units it is productively efficient but not allocatively efficient.
after.feedback: Minimum ATC establishes productive efficiency at 40. However, P exceeds MC there, so additional output has marginal value above marginal cost. Removing the cap permits P=MC at 70, establishing allocative efficiency even though ATC is above its minimum.

before.q: A competitive firm uses which cost curve to decide whether another unit should be produced?
options: Average fixed cost
Total fixed cost
Marginal cost
Accounting profit
before.feedback: The incremental output decision compares MR with MC.

after.q: A competitive firm receives $15 for one more unit and incurs $11 of extra cost. What does the marginal rule recommend?
options: Reject the unit; it lowers profit by $4.
Add the unit only if fixed cost is zero.
Add the unit; it raises profit by $4.
Reject the unit because revenue must equal total cost.
after.feedback: MR−MC=15−11=$4, so the extra unit improves profit.

before.q: Which average cost determines profit per unit after output is chosen?
options: Average variable cost
Average fixed cost
Marginal revenue
Average total cost
before.feedback: Profit per unit=P−ATC.

after.q: At its chosen output, a competitive firm has P=$24 and ATC=$19. What is profit per unit?
after.feedback: P−ATC=24−19=$5 per unit.

before.q: Which average cost determines the short-run shutdown threshold?
options: Average variable cost
Average total cost
Average fixed cost
Long-run average cost
before.feedback: AVC represents avoidable cost in the short run.

after.q: A competitive firm’s best positive output has P=$10, AVC=$8 and ATC=$13. Fixed cost is unavoidable this period. Should it operate or shut down now?
options: Operate; revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost.
Shut down; any economic loss requires immediate closure.
Operate because price exceeds ATC.
Shut down because price exceeds AVC.
after.feedback: P exceeds AVC by $2, contributing to fixed costs. Shutting down would forgo that contribution while fixed cost remains.

before.q: Why does a fixed-cost increase not change short-run competitive output?
options: It lowers MR
It does not change MC or AVC
It changes market demand
It eliminates ATC
before.feedback: Output and shutdown depend on marginal and variable costs.

after.q: A firm produces 50 units at its unique MR=MC optimum and pays an additional unavoidable $100 fixed license fee. Demand, MC and AVC are unchanged. What happens to its short-run output?
options: It rises by 100 units.
It stays at 50 units.
It falls by 2 units.
It becomes zero solely because the fee is fixed.
after.feedback: An unavoidable fixed fee changes profit but neither marginal revenue/cost nor the variable-cost shutdown comparison.

before.q: Zero economic profit includes which owner return?
options: No return at all
Only accounting depreciation
Normal profit
Consumer surplus
before.feedback: Normal profit covers entrepreneurial opportunity cost.

after.q: A firm’s revenue equals explicit costs plus $18,000 of implicit owner costs. What return is covered even though economic profit is zero?
options: An $18,000 economic profit above opportunity cost
No return on owner resources
The $18,000 normal return on owner resources
Only consumer surplus
after.feedback: The implicit $18,000 is part of economic cost and compensates the owner for the alternative forgone.

before.q: How is a competitive firm’s supply response connected to cost?
options: It follows ATC below AVC
It equals horizontal demand
It follows AFC
It follows rising MC above AVC
before.feedback: MC gives the additional cost of supply.

after.q: On its rising MC curve, a competitive firm has MC=$12 at Q=4 and MC=$15 at Q=5; AVC is below both prices. If market price rises from $12 to $15, what output change follows?
options: From 5 to 4 units
No change because all supply is fixed
Shutdown at both prices
From 4 to 5 units
after.feedback: Above the shutdown range, the firm follows rising MC: P=MC moves from Q=4 to Q=5.

before.q: What converts individual competitive firm supplies into market supply?
options: Horizontal summation at each price
Vertical summation of prices
Averaging ATC curves
Adding market demands
before.feedback: Add firm quantities supplied at each price.

after.q: At price $10, three competitive firms supply 4, 6 and 5 units. What is market quantity supplied at that price?
options: 15 units
5 units
30 units
10 units
after.feedback: Horizontal aggregation adds quantities at the same price: 4+6+5=15.

before.q: Entry affects market supply by:
options: Moving upward along the same supply curve
Shifting it to the right
Shifting demand right
Making it horizontal by definition
before.feedback: More firms supply more total output at each price.

after.q: At a given price, ten firms each supply 5 units. Two identical firms enter while existing cost curves stay fixed. What is total supply at that price afterward?
options: 50 units
60 units
12 units
70 units
after.feedback: Entry increases the number of suppliers to 12; 12×5=60 units at the given price.

before.q: Exit affects market supply by:
options: Shifting demand left
Moving down firm ATC
Shifting it to the left
Raising every firm’s fixed cost
before.feedback: Fewer firms reduce total quantity supplied.

after.q: At a given price, eight firms each supply 6 units. Two firms exit and the remaining firms’ schedules stay fixed. What is market supply at that price?
options: 48 units
12 units
36 units
60 units
after.feedback: Six remaining firms supply 6×6=36 units.

before.q: A competitive firm should expand output while:
options: ATC exceeds AVC
Price exceeds total revenue
AFC is falling
MR exceeds MC
before.feedback: Marginal benefit to the firm exceeds marginal cost.

after.q: A competitive firm receives $20 on each extra unit. The next unit costs $17 and the following one $23. Which additional output maximizes profit from these two units?
options: Add both units.
Add neither unit.
Add only the second unit.
Add only the first unit.
after.feedback: The first adds $3 to profit; the second subtracts $3. Adding only the first is best.

before.q: The last profitable unit in a discrete table is the last unit with:
options: MR at least as large as MC
ATC equal to AVC
TR equal to fixed cost
Price below AVC
before.feedback: The next unit would reduce profit once MC exceeds MR.

after.q: A price-taking firm sells at $10. The first four units cost $4, $7, $9 and $13 at the margin, respectively. Fixed cost is unavoidable. What output maximizes profit?
options: 3 units
4 units
2 units
0 units
after.feedback: The first three units each add revenue greater than cost; the fourth reduces profit by $3.

before.q: Why is the rising-MC crossing used?
options: It minimizes AFC
It is the crossing where moving beyond the output makes MC exceed MR
It sets market demand
It eliminates fixed cost
before.feedback: The local profit maximum occurs where MC rises through MR.

after.q: A firm’s MR is $10. Near output A, MC falls from $12 to $8; near output B, MC rises from $8 to $12. Which crossing gives a local profit maximum?
options: A
B
Both A and B
Neither A nor B
after.feedback: At B, marginal profit changes from positive to negative as MC crosses MR upward. A gives the opposite change.

before.q: Why is P=MC associated with allocative efficiency?
options: Profit is always zero
ATC is necessarily minimized
The marginal buyer’s value equals the marginal unit’s cost
Consumer surplus equals producer surplus
before.feedback: The last unit’s marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

after.q: The next unit is worth $22 to buyers and costs $16 to produce, with no external effects. Would adding it move toward allocative efficiency?
options: No; it destroys $6 of surplus.
No; efficiency requires minimizing AFC first.
Yes; it adds $6 of surplus.
Yes; it adds $22 of surplus regardless of cost.
after.feedback: Marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost by $6, so this additional unit increases total surplus.

before.q: A per-unit tax on competitive output directly raises:
options: Marginal and average variable cost
Only fixed cost
Only market demand
Only accounting profit
before.feedback: The tax is tied to each unit produced.

after.q: A competitive firm has MC=$9 and AVC=$7 at a specified output. A $2 tax is charged on every unit produced. What are MC and AVC at that same output after tax?
options: MC=$11 and AVC=$9
MC=$9 and AVC=$9
MC=$11 and AVC=$7
MC=$7 and AVC=$5
after.feedback: The per-unit tax adds $2 to both marginal cost and variable cost per unit.

before.q: A lump-sum annual tax on a competitive firm directly raises:
options: Marginal revenue
Average total cost but not marginal cost
Average variable cost and MC
Market demand
before.feedback: A lump-sum tax acts like fixed cost.

after.q: An unavoidable $60 annual license fee is added to a firm producing 20 units. At that output, how do ATC and MC change?
options: ATC and MC both rise by $3.
ATC rises by $3; MC is unchanged.
ATC rises by $60; MC is unchanged.
AVC and MC both rise by $60.
after.feedback: The fixed fee adds 60/20=$3 to ATC but does not change the cost of another unit.

before.q: How does the price-versus-ATC comparison connect a cost curve to the firm’s profit status?
options: ATC is irrelevant once output is chosen
The vertical gap P − ATC measures profit per unit when positive and loss per unit when negative
ATC determines marginal revenue directly
The gap P − AVC always equals total profit because fixed cost is irrelevant once the firm chooses output
before.feedback: Average total cost converts the firm’s chosen price and quantity into a per-unit economic-profit measure.

after.q: At the chosen output P=$14 and ATC=$18. What is the firm’s per-unit economic result?
options: A $4 profit
A $4 loss
An $18 loss
A $14 profit
after.feedback: P−ATC=14−18=−$4 per unit.

before.q: How does total economic profit connect the revenue and cost frameworks?
options: Profit equals total revenue minus total economic cost
Profit equals total revenue minus variable cost only
Profit equals price minus marginal cost on the last unit only
Profit equals accounting revenue plus implicit cost
before.feedback: The firm combines its revenue from price and quantity with all economic costs to measure profit.

after.q: A firm sells 30 units at $12 each and incurs $300 in total economic cost. What is total economic profit?
after.feedback: Revenue=30×12=$360; subtract $300 to obtain $60.

before.q: Why can a firm remain in long-run competitive equilibrium when economic profit is zero?
options: The firm has no opportunity costs
Zero economic profit means total revenue is zero
The government reimburses fixed costs
Revenue covers explicit and implicit costs, including normal profit
before.feedback: Normal profit is part of economic cost, so zero economic profit can still keep resources in their current use.

after.q: A firm has $100,000 revenue, $75,000 explicit costs and $25,000 implicit costs. Is zero economic profit consistent with all opportunity costs being covered?
options: No; revenue must exceed $100,000 to cover those costs.
No; implicit costs are excluded from opportunity cost.
Yes; explicit costs alone equal revenue.
Yes; revenue equals the full $100,000 economic cost.
after.feedback: 75,000+25,000=100,000. Zero economic profit includes payment for the owner’s forgone alternatives.

before.q: How does break-even connect the firm’s revenue line to its average-cost curve?
options: MR equals zero at minimum ATC
Market demand becomes perfectly inelastic
At the chosen output, price equals ATC so total revenue equals total cost
Price equals AVC so fixed cost disappears
before.feedback: Break-even is the point where the per-unit revenue and total-cost averages match.

after.q: A firm chooses Q=40 at P=$15 and ATC=$15. What are total revenue, total cost and economic profit?
options: TR=$600; TC=$600; profit=$0
TR=$600; TC=$0; profit=$600
after.feedback: Both TR and TC equal 15×40=$600, so the firm breaks even economically.

before.q: How does individual-firm supply become the competitive industry supply curve?
options: Use the market demand curve instead
Add firms’ quantities supplied at each common price
Add firms’ prices at each quantity
Average the firms’ fixed costs
before.feedback: Horizontal aggregation connects firm-level marginal-cost decisions to the market supply schedule.

after.q: At price $8, firm A supplies 3 units and firm B supplies 7. At price $10, they supply 5 and 9. What is industry quantity at price $10?
options: 10 units
14 units
24 units
20 units
after.feedback: At the common $10 price, add 5+9=14; do not add quantities from different price rows.

before.q: How does entry connect firm-level profit to a market-level supply response?
options: Entry guarantees higher long-run price
Positive economic profit attracts firms, and additional firms increase industry supply
Positive profit shifts market demand left
Entry makes each incumbent’s MC automatically fall
before.feedback: The profit signal changes the number of firms, linking firm outcomes to market supply.

after.q: Incumbents earn positive economic profit. Entry is easy, and new firms arrive while market demand stays fixed. What initial market adjustment tends to erode the profit?
options: Demand contracts because entrants buy the incumbents’ goods.
Supply expands and market price falls.
Supply contracts and market price rises.
Each incumbent’s fixed cost necessarily disappears.
after.feedback: New sellers add output at each price. With unchanged demand, the supply expansion lowers price and incumbent profit.

before.q: How does normal profit connect long-run competitive equilibrium to economic cost?
options: Normal profit is a monopoly markup above economic cost
Normal profit is excluded from economic cost
Normal profit exists only when P exceeds ATC
Normal profit is the implicit return required to keep owner resources in the industry
before.feedback: Zero economic profit can be sustainable because normal profit is already included among opportunity costs.

after.q: An owner requires $30,000 to match the best alternative use of its resources. The business earns exactly that amount after explicit costs. What are normal profit and economic profit?
options: Normal profit=$0; economic profit=$30,000
Both equal $30,000
Both equal $0
Normal profit=$30,000; economic profit=$0
after.feedback: The $30,000 covers implicit opportunity cost. Economic profit is the amount above that required return, here zero.

before.q: A rising price and rising quantity most strongly suggest which change, other things equal?
options: A decrease in demand.
An increase in demand.
An increase in supply.
A binding price floor becoming lower.
before.feedback: An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity, other things equal.

after.q: Price and quantity both rise. A report concludes that demand increased and that supply could not have changed. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: Only a supply increase fits because more output always means greater supply.
A demand increase alone fits the observations, but simultaneous supply changes are possible; the two observations do not identify every shift.
Only a supply decrease fits because a higher price always means reduced supply.
Demand and supply must both be unchanged because equilibrium quantities cannot rise together with price.
after.feedback: A rightward demand shift raises both price and quantity with supply fixed. But combined shifts can produce the same observed directions, so the evidence supports a possible explanation rather than uniquely identifying every determinant.

before.q: A market loss most directly encourages resources to:
options: Remain permanently in the same activity.
Ignore production costs.
Move toward alternative uses with higher expected value.
Increase quantity demanded.
before.feedback: Persistent losses signal that the resources used in this activity may create greater value elsewhere, encouraging them to move toward alternative uses.

after.q: Resources currently used in a product would generate next year’s revenue of $120 and total opportunity cost of $140. An alternative use would generate revenue of $90 and opportunity cost of $70. Past spending is unrecoverable. Which allocation follows from the expected net-value signals?
options: Stay because $120 revenue exceeds the alternative’s $90, even though opportunity cost is higher.
Stay until past spending is recovered because sunk costs determine the best future use.
Move to the alternative: expected net value improves from −$20 to +$20, regardless of unrecoverable past spending.
Move only if the alternative’s revenue exceeds $140, ignoring its lower opportunity cost.
after.feedback: The current use has net value 120−140=−20; the alternative has 90−70=20. The $40 improvement concerns future alternatives. Unrecoverable past spending does not change that comparison.

before.q: A congestion toll is intended to communicate:
options: That road space is unlimited.
That every trip has equal value.
That supply of roads rises instantly.
The additional delay cost created by using the road at busy times.
before.feedback: A congestion toll makes drivers face more of the additional delay cost their trip imposes on others during busy periods.

after.q: A trip gives a driver benefit $6, uses $3 of private resources and imposes $4 of delay on others. A congestion toll equals the external delay cost and its collection uses no resources. Which prediction explains the corrected price signal?
options: The driver takes the trip because the $4 toll is a transfer and therefore cannot affect private incentives.
The driver declines because the toll creates $4 of additional social resource cost beyond the original delay.
The driver takes the trip because only the $3 private resource use can enter the efficiency comparison.
The driver faces $7 in private cost plus toll and declines the trip; this avoids a trip whose $7 social resource cost exceeds its $6 benefit.
after.feedback: Without the toll the driver sees benefit 6 versus private cost 3. The $4 toll makes the private comparison reflect the $7 social cost. The payment is a transfer in welfare accounting, but it changes the driver’s incentive.
